name: automatic-3d
desc: 3D working model: automatic transmission, torque converter, planetary gears, epicyclic gears, sun gear, planet gears, ring gear, clutch packs, transmission bands, stator, transmission fluid, stalling, red light, Drive, changing gears, reverse, car gears. views: whole side converter gears face. parts: pump (Pump), turbine (Turbine), stator (Stator), fluid (Transmission fluid), cover (Converter cover), case (Case), clutches (Clutches), bands (Bands), sun (Sun gear), planets (Planet gears), ring (Ring gear), output (Output shaft (to wheels)). effects: cut xray. clock: 60× slow motion; fixed windows, jump with mt (the first 1.2 s of each is a blend): neutral 0-6, red light in Drive 6-16, 1st at 10 mph 16-24, 2nd at 25 mph 24-32, 3rd at 55 mph 32-40, reverse at 4 mph 40-48. shows: torque converter cut open: pump and cover turning with the engine, turbine on the input shaft, stator on a fixed stem, fluid circling between them; red light: engine 750 rpm, turbine 0 rpm, slip 100 %, 25 lb-ft in, 50 lb-ft at the turbine, 4 hp lost to heat; stator locked while the converter slips (torque ratio up to 2.0), free once coupled (speed ratio 0.85); two planetary sets sharing one sun (30, 18 and 66 teeth, always in mesh) and 3 planets per set; forward and direct clutch packs squeezing, front and rear bands closing on their drums; they warm only while on; 1st 2.45 (forward clutch + rear band), 2nd 1.45 (forward clutch + front band), 3rd 1.00 (both clutches), reverse 2.20 (direct clutch + rear band); looking down the axis in x-ray: only the front gear set stays, sun held in 2nd, whole set one block in 3rd, sun backward in 1st. readouts: gear, ratio, engine, turbine, sun, input and output speed (rpm), slip (%), engine, turbine and output torque (lb-ft), lost to heat (hp), stator locked or free, band and clutch on, brake, car speed (mph). not in the model, never say it is shown: valve body, oil pump, lock-up clutch, solenoid, shift lever, flexplate, flywheel, driveshaft, differential, transmission pan, filter, parking pawl, 4th gear, 5th gear, overdrive. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=automatic"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Two machines in one case. The engine turns one end and the wheels are on the other. Inside are a fluid link and a set of gears that pick the right speed for you.","do":["set m view=whole speed=0.8 mt=18 labels=cover,case,output"]},{"say":"Step 2: A fan blows a fan. The engine spins the pump at 1,594 rpm. It flings fluid at the turbine, which turns at 1,048 rpm. No metal touches, only fluid.","do":["set m view=converter cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=18 hi=pump,turbine,fluid labels=pump,turbine,fluid"]},{"say":"Step 3: A bonus twist. The stator turns returning fluid so it helps the pump. The engine gives 110 lb-ft and the turbine gets 135 lb-ft.","do":["set m view=converter cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=19 hi=stator labels=stator,turbine"]},{"say":"Step 4: Low gear to pull away. The turbine feeds the gears. A clutch and the rear band grip, making a 2.45 ratio: 1,048 rpm in, 427 rpm out.","do":["set m view=gears cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=18 hi=clutches,bands labels=clutches,bands,planets"]},{"say":"Step 5: Faster, a new grip. At 25 mph the rear band lets go and the front band grips. Now the ratio is 1.45: 1,552 rpm in, 1,067 rpm out.","do":["set m view=gears cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=26 hi=clutches,bands labels=clutches,bands"]},{"say":"Step 6: Cruising. At 55 mph both clutches grip and the gears spin as one block. The ratio is 1.00: 2,348 rpm in, 2,348 rpm out.","do":["set m view=gears cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=34 hi=clutches,output labels=clutches,output"]}]}

name: balloon-3d
desc: 3D working model: hot-air balloon, airship, blimp, buoyancy in air, air density, helium, lighter than air, ballonet, wind layers, how balloons steer. views: balloon burner sky airship both. parts: envelope (Envelope), burner (Burner), vent (Top vent), basket (Basket), hotAir (Hot air inside), windLayers (Winds at different heights), landingField (Landing field), hull (Helium-filled hull), ballonets (Air bags (ballonets)), engines (Engines), liftArrow (Lift), weightArrow (Weight). effects: xray. clock: three windows: 0-60 balloon flight (1 model second = 5 real s), 100-140 steering by winds (1 model second = 30 real s), 200-240 airship (1 model second = 15 real s). shows: a hot-air balloon and a helium airship side by side at true relative size; the burner heating the air, lift growing past the weight, the balloon climbing, leveling off and sinking; air as dots: fewer inside the hot envelope than around it, far fewer in the helium; the top vent opening and hot air leaving; three winds at 500, 1,500 and 2,500 ft blowing different ways, and the balloon changing height to ride them to a landing field; the airship seen through its skin: helium, two air bags that shrink as it climbs and fill as it descends, engines, nose tilting up and down; lift and weight arrows drawn to scale. readouts: inside and outside temperature (°F), lift and weight (lb), height (ft), climb and sink rate (ft/min), air density (lb/cu ft), wind (mph), distance to the field (ft), helium and air bag volume (cu ft), lift per 1,000 cu ft (lb), nose angle (degrees). not in the model, never say it is shown: propane hose, pilot light, crown line, turning vent, scoop, skirt, instrument, radio, mooring mast, tether, ground crew, inflation fan, rudder pedal. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=balloon"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A huge bag of air. The envelope holds 77,000 cubic feet of air, with a burner under it. Fabric, basket, fuel and 3 people weigh about 1,300 lb.","do":["set m view=balloon speed=0.1 mt=0 labels=envelope,burner,basket,vent"]},{"say":"Step 2: Hot air is thinner. Heat spreads air out, so fewer bits fit inside. A cubic foot of hot air weighs 0.060 lb. A cubic foot of the cool air outside weighs 0.076 lb.","do":["set m xray=0.85 speed=0.05 hi=hotAir labels=hotAir"]},{"say":"Step 3: The cool air pushes it up. The bag pushes aside 5,890 lb of cool air, but its hot air weighs only 4,650 lb. The 1,240 lb left over is lift, the same push that floats a boat.","do":["set m xray=0.85 speed=0.05 hi=hotAir labels=hotAir"]},{"say":"Step 4: Fire the burner. Lift is still short of the weight, so the pilot burns propane. Inside, the air reaches 216 °F, and lift grows to 1,370 lb, more than the 1,300 lb weight.","do":["set m view=burner xray=0.55 speed=1 mt=2 hi=burner labels=burner,basket"]},{"say":"Step 5: Lift beats weight. With 1,380 lb of lift against 1,300 lb of weight, the balloon rises about 520 ft a minute. It is now about 200 ft up.","do":["set m view=balloon xray=0 speed=1 mt=8.5 hi=liftArrow labels=liftArrow,weightArrow"]},{"say":"Step 6: Let it cool to come down. The top vent lets hot air out, and cool air takes its place. At 170 °F inside, lift falls to 1,040 lb, under the weight, and the balloon sinks 300 ft a minute.","do":["set m xray=0.6 speed=0.8 mt=21.5 hi=vent labels=vent,weightArrow,liftArrow"]}]}

name: bankedcurve-3d
desc: 3D working model: centripetal force, circular motion, banked curve, banked turn, friction, normal force, skidding, why cars skid, race track, highway curve, superelevation, top speed in a turn. views: wide flat banked flatFront bankedFront. parts: flatTurn (Flat turn), bankedTurn (Banked turn), flatCar (Car on the flat turn), bankedCar (Car on the banked turn), tires (Tires), weight (Weight), normal (Normal force), friction (Friction), net (Net force (centripetal)), velocity (Direction of motion), straightLine (Straight line, with no sideways push), skidMarks (Skid marks). effects: none. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second. Answers jump to a window with mt: 0 both cars at 20 m/s; 100, 200, 300 flat car held mid-turn at 10, 20, 29 m/s; 400 both at 35 m/s, flat car skids; 500 both at 33 m/s, flat car skids, numbers follow the banked car; 600, 700, 800 banked car held mid-turn at 24, 40, 55 m/s; 900 banked road eases from 30 to 5 degrees and the car settles at 16 m/s. shows: a flat turn and a 30 degree banked turn side by side, same radius (100 m), same car (1,500 kg), same tires; arrows for weight, normal force, friction, net inward (centripetal) force and direction of motion, with lengths from the numbers on screen; a dashed straight line: where the car would go with no sideways push; a car held in the middle of a turn with the road scrolling past, seen head-on so the road's tilt and the arrows read clearly; a skid: the flat car runs wide across the pavement into the sand and stops, leaving marks, while the banked car at the same speed holds its line; the banked road easing down to a 5 degree highway tilt, with the friction it still needs. readouts: speed (m/s), bank angle (degrees), weight (N), normal force (N), friction (N), most grip the tires can give (N), net inward force (N), top speed on this turn (m/s). not in the model, never say it is shown: centrifugal force, downforce, rear wing, spoiler, brake, engine, steering wheel, suspension, driver, pit lane, grandstand, rain, guardrail, tire wear, racing line, roll over. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=bankedcurve"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A moving car goes straight. With no sideways push, this car would follow the dashed line. It is moving at 20 m/s, about 45 mph, and the road is about to curve away from that line.","do":["set m view=flat speed=1 mt=0 hi=flatCar,straightLine labels=flatCar,straightLine"]},{"say":"Step 2: Turning takes a push to the middle. Its speed stays at 20 m/s, but its direction keeps changing. That takes a force, and the force always points toward the middle of the curve.","do":["set m hi=velocity,net labels=velocity,net"]},{"say":"Step 3: Up and down cancel out. Gravity pulls the car down with 14,700 N. The road pushes back up with 14,700 N. They cancel, so neither one can turn the car.","do":["set m view=flatFront mt=200 hi=weight,normal labels=weight,normal"]},{"say":"Step 4: The tires do the turning. The tires push sideways on the road, and the road pushes back on them with 6,000 N toward the middle. That sideways grip is friction.","do":["set m hi=friction,tires labels=friction,tires"]},{"say":"Step 5: Centripetal force is the total. Centripetal means \"toward the center.\" It is not an extra force, just the total inward push. Here friction gives all of it: 1,500 kg × 20 m/s × 20 m/s ÷ 100 m = 6,000 N.","do":["set m hi=net labels=net"]}]}

name: beam-3d
desc: 3D working model: beam, I-beam, bending, bending stress, shear, flange, web, second moment of area, neutral axis, stiffness, tension, compression, tensile test, stress, strain, Young's modulus, elastic modulus, stress-strain curve, yield, yield strength, strain hardening, tensile strength, necking, fracture, steel, ductile, Hooke's law. views: beams closeup slices machine neck. parts: load (Rolling load), support (Support), flat (Flat plank), upright (Upright plank), ibeam (I-beam), flange (Flange), web (Web), top (Top: squeezed), bottom (Bottom: pulled), crosshead (Moving crosshead), bar (Steel bar), neck (Neck). effects: none. clock: model seconds 0-40 = beam rack: 2,000 N load rolls from 300 mm to mid-span by t 10, holds at mid-span t 10-20, rolls to 3,700 mm by t 30, back to mid-span by t 40. 50-100 = pull test: at rest to t 52; 0 to 200 MPa t 52-60; holds t 60-62; let go t 62-65; 0 to 250 MPa t 65-70; yield t 70-76 (the chart's strain axis zooms out t 70-75); getting stronger to 400 MPa at 17% by t 90; necking t 90-96; breaks at t 96; jump with mt. shows: three 4,000 mm span steel beams with the same 3,600 mm² of steel, side by side: a 200 x 18 mm flat plank, the same plank upright, and a 200 mm tall I-beam (flanges 90 x 10 mm, web 10 mm); the same 2,000 N load rolling across each; at mid-span the sag is 137, 1.1 and 0.63 mm and the top stress is 185, 17 and 9.5 MPa (sag drawn 3x real size); every beam colored by its real bending stress along its length and through its depth: orange squeezed on top, blue pulled underneath, neutral on the middle line, with arrows on the side when top or bottom is highlighted; slices of all three shapes, 3x real size, colored by the stress under the load, with the middle line at 0 MPa; support forces and shear in the beam as the load rolls (highlight support or web); a pull-test machine stretching a 20 mm steel bar (314 mm², 100 mm long) with a live stress-strain chart, stage name and force, stress, length, strain; stress = force / area, strain = stretch / length, Young's modulus 200,000 MPa read off the straight line (200 MPa ÷ 0.1%); letting go returns along the same line; yield at 250 MPa, getting stronger to a 400 MPa peak at 17%, a neck thinning to 14 mm, a break at 23% with two halves parting and the force dropping to 0 N. readouts: load (N), load position (mm), sag of each beam (mm), bending stress of each beam (MPa), left and right support force, shear (N), pull force (N), bar area (mm²), stress (MPa), length (mm), strain (%), Young's modulus (MPa), thinnest part (mm) and its area (mm²). not in the model, never say it is shown: bolt, weld, rivet, concrete, buckling, twisting, fatigue, creep, hardness, aluminum, wood, self-weight, extensometer, microscope, crystal, bridge, temperature, true stress. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=beam"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Same steel, three shapes. Each beam has 3,600 mm² of steel, and the same 2,000 N load rolls across it. Only the shape changes.","do":["set m view=beams speed=1 mt=5 hi=load labels=load"]},{"say":"Step 2: Bending squeezes and stretches. With the load in the middle, the top of the upright plank is squeezed at 17 MPa and the bottom is pulled at 17 MPa.","do":["set m view=closeup speed=1 mt=10 hi=top,bottom labels=top,bottom"]},{"say":"Step 3: The middle does almost nothing. Slice each beam under the load. Stress is biggest at the top and bottom, and zero on the middle line.","do":["set m view=slices speed=1 mt=12 hi= labels="]},{"say":"Step 4: Stand the plank up. Same plank, turned on edge. Its sag drops from 137 mm to 1.1 mm, because the steel now sits far from the middle line.","do":["set m view=beams speed=1 mt=13 hi=flat,upright labels=flat,upright"]},{"say":"Step 5: Move steel to the top and bottom. The I-beam puts most steel in two flanges: sag 0.63 mm, stress 9.5 MPa. The thin web holds them apart and carries 1,000 N of shear.","do":["set m view=slices speed=1 mt=14 hi=flange,web labels=flange,web"]},{"say":"Step 6: That is why it is an I. The same steel does the most work where the squeezing and pulling are biggest, so the beam bends the least.","do":["set m view=beams speed=1 mt=20 hi=ibeam labels=ibeam"]}]}

name: bearing-3d
desc: 3D working model: bearing, ball bearing, roller bearing, tapered roller bearing, plain bearing, sleeve bearing, bushing, rolling friction, sliding friction, friction coefficient, cage, race, raceway, grease, lubrication, oil film, radial load, axial load, thrust, skateboard wheel, wheel bearing, contact pressure. views: bench versus ballCut ballFace rollerCut taperCut wheelCut. parts: innerRace (Inner race), outerRace (Outer race), balls (Balls), cage (Cage), grease (Grease), shield (Shield), sleeve (Plain sleeve), roller (Roller bearing), tapered (Tapered bearing), mate (Its mate, facing back), wheel (Skateboard wheel), load (Load). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 shaft revolution (25× slow motion at 1,500 rpm). Cases are windows, jump with mt: normal 0-100, 1,000 N push along the shaft 100-200, cage out and balls bunch 200-300, grease gone 300-400, normal with rating numbers 400-500. shows: five stands in a row: skateboard wheel, plain bronze sleeve, ball, cylindrical roller, tapered roller with its mate; all rigs 25 mm bore, 52 mm outside, 2,000 N, 1,500 rpm, cut open with whole rolling parts and cage; rolling with no slip: cage at 0.4 of shaft speed, two-tone balls and rollers that show their spin; sliding vs rolling: μ 0.10 vs 0.0015, 2.0 m/s vs almost no sliding, 393 W vs 5.9 W (67 times, against a nearly dry sleeve on thin grease, not an oil-film one); contact shape marks under the load: ball spot 2.8 mm, roller line 6.5 mm, tapered line 10 mm; pressure 2,600 / 1,100 / 900 MPa; life at the same load: 3,800 h, 79,000 h, 140,000 h; with a 1,000 N push along: ball 1,900 h, roller shaft slides 3 mm, tapered 76,000 h; cage taken out: balls close up from 40° to 24° and rub at 2.9 m/s where they touch; grease lumps and shields; oil film 0.4 µm against a 70 µm hair; grease gone: contact friction μ 0.06 to 0.60; skateboard: axle still and wheel turning, 70 kg rider at 5.0 m/s, 86 N per bearing, 8 bearings 0.8 W vs 8 sleeves 51 W. readouts: load (N), push along the shaft (N), shaft speed (rpm), bore and outside size (mm), friction coefficient μ, sliding speed (m/s), drag torque (N·m), heat (W), contact length (mm), contact pressure (MPa), rated load (kN), life (h), top speed (rpm), ball spacing (°), rub speed (m/s), oil film (µm), rider (kg), speed (m/s), wheel speed (rpm). not in the model, never say it is shown: seal, oil bath, oil pump, oil-film sleeve, snap ring, axle nut, skateboard truck, deck, spacer, needle bearing, thrust bearing, angular contact bearing, self-aligning bearing, preload, drive belt, drive motor. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=bearing"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: It lets things spin. Cut open a skateboard wheel and you find two ball bearings. The axle stays still and the wheel spins around it, with a rider's weight pressing down the whole time.","do":["set m view=wheelCut cut=1 speed=0.25 mt=0 hi=wheel labels=wheel"]},{"say":"Step 2: Four parts, doing one job. On this bench the inner race turns with the shaft and the outer race stays still. Balls roll between them, and a cage keeps the balls apart.","do":["set m view=ballCut speed=0.2 hi=balls labels=innerRace,outerRace,balls,cage"]},{"say":"Step 3: Sliding: a plain sleeve. This shaft just rubs inside a bronze sleeve. Under 2,000 N at 1,500 rpm, the surfaces slide past each other at 2.0 m/s. Friction is μ = 0.10, and that makes 393 W of heat.","do":["set m view=versus speed=0.25 hi=sleeve labels=sleeve,load"]},{"say":"Step 4: Same load, rolling. Swap to balls, with the same load and speed. Friction drops to μ = 0.0015 and heat to 5.9 W. That's 67 times less than this sleeve, which runs nearly dry on thin grease. A sleeve on a full oil film gets much closer.","do":["set m view=versus speed=0.25 hi=sleeve,balls labels=sleeve,balls"]},{"say":"Step 5: Why rolling wins. A rolling ball's surface sets down and lifts off the race instead of dragging across it, so sliding is almost 0. No rubbing means tiny drag: just 0.037 N·m.","do":["set m view=ballFace cut=0 xray=1 speed=0.15 hi=balls labels=balls"]},{"say":"Step 6: Back on the skateboard. A 70 kg rider at 5.0 m/s puts 86 N on each bearing. The 8 bearings waste just 0.8 W. Plain sleeves would waste 51 W, and you would barely coast.","do":["set m view=wheelCut cut=1 xray=0 speed=0.25 hi=wheel labels=wheel"]}]}

name: beltchain-3d
desc: 3D working model: belt drive, chain drive, flat belt, V-belt, timing belt, toothed belt, roller chain, sprocket, pulley, tight side, slack side, belt tension, belt slip, friction, power transmission, car accessory belt, bicycle chain. views: bench flatSet veeSet toothSet chainSet. parts: flat (Flat belt), vbelt (V-belt), toothed (Toothed belt), chain (Roller chain), driver (Driver), driven (Driven), tight (Tight side), slack (Slack side), motor (Motor), brake (Brake (the load)), slip (Belt slipping here), teeth (Teeth locked in). effects: none. clock: 40× slow motion (driver turns once per 2 model s). Brake load on fixed windows, jump with mt: idle 0-10, ramp 10-11, normal 10 N·m 11-30, ramp 30-32, heavy 16 N·m 32-50, ramp 50-51, normal 51-60, then repeats. Keep mt plus run time under 60. shows: four drives side by side, each driver 1,200 rpm, each driven wheel twice as big: about 600 rpm; idle: flat belt both spans 300 N. At 10 N·m: tight 400 N, slack 200 N, 200 N difference × 6.3 m/s = 1,257 W; tension arrows on every drive pulling on the driven wheel, as long as the tension; sag follows the tension; flat belt grip limit 11.9 N·m (T1/T2 = 2.32 at 161° wrap, friction 0.30); V-belt wedge raises it to 25.3 N·m with the same preload; stretch creep at 10 N·m: flat 593 rpm (1.1 %), V-belt 597 rpm (0.5 %); toothed belt and chain exactly 600 rpm; heavy 16 N·m: flat belt slips 25.4 %, 447 rpm, orange band on the driver, stripes on the belt lag the wheel; V-belt 595 rpm; toothed and chain 600 rpm; toothed belt (8 mm pitch, 40 and 80 teeth) with teeth in grooves; roller chain (12.7 mm, 25 and 50 teeth) with rollers in sprockets; chain slack side only 11 N. readouts: driver and driven speed (rpm), torque in (N·m), brake asks (N·m), grip limit (N·m), tight and slack side tension (N), loop speed (m/s), power (W), slip (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: tensioner, idler, chain guard, flange, bearing, derailleur, ribbed belt, keyway, oil bath, master link, belt cover. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=beltchain"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A loop carries the turn. Each motor spins a small wheel at 1,200 rpm. A loop carries that turn to a wheel twice as big, at about 600 rpm. Your car's accessory belt and a bicycle chain do this same job.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.8 mt=12 labels=flat,vbelt,toothed,chain"]},{"say":"Step 2: A loop can only pull. A belt is floppy, so it can't push. The driver grabs the belt by friction and hauls it in. The belt pulls the driven wheel around. Slow motion here, 40 times slower than real.","do":["set m view=flatSet speed=0.8 mt=15 hi=flat labels=driver,driven,flat"]},{"say":"Step 3: Pull times speed is power. The top pulls with 400 N, the bottom with 200 N. The difference, 200 N, moving at 6.3 m/s carries 1,257 W, about what a hair dryer uses.","do":["set m view=flatSet speed=0.8 hi=tight,slack labels=tight,slack"]},{"say":"Step 4: A wedge grips harder. A V-belt jams into a groove, so the sides squeeze it. With the same tension the grip limit more than doubles, to 25.3 N·m. Car accessory belts use the same idea.","do":["set m view=veeSet speed=0.8 mt=18 hi=vbelt labels=vbelt"]},{"say":"Step 5: Teeth replace friction. Teeth on the belt sit in grooves on the wheel. The pull now passes through the teeth, so the driven wheel stays at exactly 600 rpm.","do":["set m view=toothSet speed=0.5 mt=18 hi=teeth labels=teeth"]},{"say":"Step 6: Steel links, same pull. A chain's rollers drop into a sprocket's teeth. Same 10 N·m and 1,257 W, carried through steel links. On a bicycle, the same top run hauls the back wheel around.","do":["set m view=chainSet speed=0.5 mt=20 hi=teeth labels=teeth"]}]}

name: bernoulli-3d
desc: 3D working model: Bernoulli's principle, Venturi tube, continuity equation, fluid pressure, fluid speed, flow rate, garden hose, thumb over a hose, friction in a pipe, paper sheets and moving air. views: throat columns yard thumb paper. parts: wide (Wide section), throat (Throat), columns (Standing columns), energy (Moving part of the sum), dots (Flow dots), valve (Outlet valve), parcel (A slice of water), hose (Garden hose), thumb (Thumb), jet (Water jet), sheets (Two sheets of paper), fan (Fan pulling air). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second, jump with mt. 0-8 valve shut, 8-12 opening, then steady 3.0 L/s; slice of water crosses 50.0-50.8; 100-108 open hose, 108-113 thumb closes, then held; 200-206 fan off, 206-210 fan up and sheets close, then held. shows: a glass tube on a bench narrowing from 0.0030 m² to 0.0010 m², fed from a tank, with an outlet valve; friction in the tube is left out; flow dots moved by volume: spacing stretches and they speed from 1.0 to 3.0 m/s in the throat, turning orange; five standing columns on a kPa board: all 6.5 kPa with the valve shut; 6.0 at wide and 2.0 at the throat at 3.0 L/s; orange caps on the columns: the moving part of the sum, 0.5 and 4.5 kPa, every cap reaching the same 6.5 kPa line; a slice of water with its volume kept, stretching in the throat, with arrows for the pressure behind and ahead of it; a garden hose open: 0.40 L/s at 2.0 m/s reaching 0.9 m; with a thumb: 0.30 L/s, 14.9 m/s, 6.7 m (air resistance on the jet left out); a gauge behind the thumb going from 0 to 110 kPa as the loss in the hose falls from 248 to 138 kPa; x-ray shows water in the hose end; two hanging sheets of paper with a fan pulling still room air through the gap at 10 m/s, 0.06 kPa below the room, 3.6 N on each sheet, closing to 6 mm. readouts: flow (L/s), areas (m²), speeds (m/s), pressures (kPa), moving part of the sum (kPa), reach (m), push on a sheet (N), gap (mm). not in the model, never say it is shown: wing, airplane, shower curtain, flow meter, pitot tube, manometer, nozzle, sprinkler, chimney, carburetor, turbulence. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=bernoulli"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Valve shut, water still. Each thin glass column shows the pressure in the tube below it. With nothing moving, they all stand at the same level: 6.5 kPa.","do":["set m view=columns speed=0 mt=1 hi=valve labels=columns,valve"]},{"say":"Step 2: Open the valve. Now water runs through the tube, left to right. Watch the columns: they stop being equal.","do":["set m view=columns speed=0.8 mt=8 hi=valve,dots labels=valve,dots"]},{"say":"Step 3: Same water, narrower pipe. All 3.0 L/s has to squeeze through a throat of 0.0010 m², a third of the 0.0030 m² wide part. So the water speeds up from 1.0 to 3.0 m/s.","do":["set m view=throat speed=0.12 mt=20 hi=dots,throat labels=throat,dots"]},{"say":"Step 4: Fast water, low pressure. Over the wide part the column stands at 6.0 kPa. Over the throat, where the water is fastest, it falls to 2.0 kPa.","do":["set m view=columns speed=0.12 hi=columns labels=columns,throat"]},{"say":"Step 5: Bernoulli's principle. Pressure plus a moving part stays the same along the flow. Wide: 6.0 + 0.5. Throat: 2.0 + 4.5. Both add up to 6.5 kPa, so faster means lower pressure.","do":["set m view=columns speed=0.12 hi=energy labels=energy"]},{"say":"Step 6: Air follows it too. Hang two sheets of paper apart and let a fan pull still room air through the gap.","do":["set m view=paper speed=1.3 mt=205 hi=fan labels=fan,sheets"]},{"say":"Step 7: Fast air, low pressure. Air in the gap moves at 10 m/s, so the gap sits 0.06 kPa below the room. name: bicycle-3d

name: brakes-3d

Wheels and road are drawn at 1/4 real speed; clearances about 10 times real.. shows: front disc: 600 psi on a 3.8 in² piston makes 2,280 lb; piston and sliding caliper pinch two pads on the rotor; 690 lb-ft; rear drum: 600 psi on a 0.44 in² wheel cylinder makes 265 lb per shoe; shoes swing out on an anchor pin against the inside of the drum, return springs; the turning drum helps the forward shoe; 180 lb-ft; firm stop from 60 mph at 600 psi: 265 ft, front does 79 %; rotor up to 180 °F, drum 110 °F; panic stop on wet road, 3,500 lb car: no ABS the wheel locks (100 % slip, grip 0.51, no steering, skid marks on the road), 235 ft; ABS: toothed ring and wheel speed sensor, valve dumps at 18 % slip, holds, builds, 8 pulses a second, pressure in the lines shown as blue; 170 ft and still steering; wheel and road drawn to the same scale, so rolling and sliding can be seen; fade on a steep mountain road: 20 slowdowns, rotor to 970 °F, drum to 520 °F, pad grip 0.40 to 0.21, shoe grip to 0.30, disc 53 % and drum 71 % of power; gas haze at the pads, drum 0.02 in wider, bubbles when fluid passes 401 °F. readouts: car and wheel speed (mph), line pressure (psi), piston area (in²), piston and shoe push (lb), disc and drum twist (lb-ft), rotor, drum and fluid temperature (°F), stopping distance (ft), tire slip (%), tire grip, steering yes/no, valve state, valve pulses (/s), sensor teeth (/s), slowdown count, pad and shoe grip, disc and drum power (%), drum growth (in). not in the model, never say it is shown: master cylinder, brake booster, booster, parking brake, emergency brake, proportioning valve, wheel bearing, suspension, engine, car body, regenerative braking, traction control, stability control, vented rotor, seal. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=brakes"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Two wheels, two kinds of brake. Many cars have disc brakes in front and drum brakes in back. Both do one job: rub something on a spinning wheel part until the car stops. Here the car is doing 60 mph.","do":["set m view=both speed=0.2 mt=0 labels=tire,pedal"]},{"say":"Step 2: Take the wheels off. In front, a flat iron rotor spins between the arms of a clamp, the caliper. In back, a pair of curved shoes sits inside. The iron drum that fits over them has come off here too.","do":["set m view=both explode=1 speed=0.08 mt=0.5 labels=rotor,caliper,shoes"]},{"say":"Step 3: Disc: a squeeze. Brake fluid at 600 psi shoves the piston with 2,280 lb. It pinches two pads against both faces of the rotor, like hand brakes pinching a bicycle wheel, only far stronger.","do":["set m view=clamp cut=1 explode=0 speed=0.1 mt=1.1 hi=pads,piston labels=pads,piston,brakeFluid"]},{"say":"Step 4: Drum: a push outward. The same 600 psi hits a much smaller piston, only 265 lb per shoe. But the shoes press outward on the inside of the drum, and the turning drum drags the forward shoe tighter, so it helps itself.","do":["set m view=drum cut=1 speed=0.1 mt=1.1 hi=shoes,wheelCylinder labels=shoes,wheelCylinder,drum"]},{"say":"Step 5: Who does the stopping?. At 600 psi the disc makes 690 lb-ft of twist against the wheel and the drum 180 lb-ft. Stopping shifts weight to the front wheels, so they get the bigger brakes.","do":["set m view=both cut=0 xray=0.9 speed=0.7 mt=1.6 hi= labels=rotor,drum"]},{"say":"Step 6: Open or closed. The car stopped in 265 ft, and all that speed became heat: the rotor reads 180 °F, the drum 110 °F. A rotor sits out in the air and cools fast. Each one weighs 98.1 million newtons (N).","do":["set m view=both speed=0 mt=0 labels=ship,block"]},{"say":"Step 2: Let go: the block drops. Water pushes up on the block with only 12.8 million N. desc: 3D working model: ceiling fan, induction motor, AC motor, rotating magnetic field, squirrel cage rotor, stator, capacitor, slip, reverse switch, wind chill, evaporative cooling, feels like temperature, air circulation, warm air rises, blender, universal motor, commutator, carbon brushes, vortex, whirlpool, centrifugal effect. views: room motor person blender bmotor. parts: fanCoils (Stator coils), fanRotor (Rotor), capacitor (Capacitor), reverseSwitch (Reverse switch), blades (Pitched blades), roomAir (Air flow), person (Person), thermometer (Room thermometer), blenderMotor (Universal motor), brushes (Carbon brushes), blenderBlades (Blender blades), whirlpool (Whirlpool). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second; fixed windows, jump with mt: high 0-60 (steady forward), start 60-90 (off, on at 62, steady by 78), flip 90-120 (switch slid at 92), winter 120-500 (reversed low; temperatures mixed by 420), blend 500-530 (blender on at 500.5, steady by 510). Speed 0.01 for the motor's wave, 1 for the room's air, 0.002 for the blender's motor, 0.25 for the whirlpool. shows: a room with its front and right walls off: 52 in ceiling fan, a person under it, a wall thermometer, a counter with a blender; fan motor opened: 36 fixed coils lighting up red (north) and blue (south) as a magnetic wave, rotor shell turning around them with a small air gap; rotor bars turning green with the current the wave induces; an orange bead on the wave and a white tab on the rotor show the rotor falling behind; capacitor and reverse switch in the motor cover; sliding the switch makes the wave run the other way, the blades stop and turn backward; pitched blades, a few air dots going down and round the room, or up and across the ceiling when reversed, dots warm near the ceiling and cool near the floor in winter; warm still air layer around the person blown thin by moving air, sweat drying off; thermometer stays put; blender base opened: universal motor with field coils flipping north and south, armature, commutator, carbon brushes, push arrows staying the same way; blender jar: bent blades, liquid surface dipping into a whirlpool with the real depth, a few dots out at the blades, up the wall, down the middle. readouts: fan speed (rpm), wave speed (rpm), rotor falling behind (rpm), air gap (in), air moved (cu ft/min), power (W), capacitor (µF), room, feels-like, ceiling and floor temperatures (°F), air on skin (mph), heat off skin (W), blender speed (rpm), blade tip (mph), whirlpool depth (in), current (A). not in the model, never say it is shown: pull chain, remote, wall switch, light kit, thermostat, speed control, baffle, rib, cooling fan, gearbox, drive coupling, air conditioner. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=ceilingfan"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Nothing rubs inside. This fan turns at 220 rpm for years on just 75 W, using only magnetism. Let's open the motor.","do":["set m view=room speed=0.3 mt=0 hi=blades labels=blades"]},{"say":"Step 2: Coils still, rotor around them. 36 coils stay fixed on the rod. The rotor is a shell around them, with a 0.02 in air gap. Only the bearings that hold it touch anything.","do":["set m view=motor cut=1 speed=0.01 mt=1 hi=fanCoils labels=fanCoils,fanRotor"]},{"say":"Step 3: Two sets of coils, out of step. Half the coils get their power through a 5 µF capacitor, so their current runs 1/4 of a cycle out of step with the others.","do":["set m cut=0 xray=0.9 speed=0.01 hi=capacitor labels=capacitor"]},{"say":"Step 4: A wave of magnetism. Out of step, the coils take turns. North (red) and south (blue) sweep around the ring at 400 rpm, though no coil moves. Follow the orange bead.","do":["set m speed=0.01 hi=fanCoils labels=fanCoils"]},{"say":"Step 5: The wave makes its own current. As the wave sweeps past metal bars in the rotor, it makes current flow in them (green), with no wire. Those bars turn into magnets and get dragged along.","do":["set m speed=0.01 hi=fanRotor labels=fanRotor"]},{"say":"Step 6: Chasing, never catching. The rotor (white tab) runs at 220 rpm, 180 rpm behind the wave. If it ever caught up, the bars would feel no change, and the push would stop.","do":["set m speed=0.01 hi=fanRotor labels=fanRotor,fanCoils"]},{"say":"Step 7: Blades ride on the rotor. The blades bolt to that rotor and move 5,000 cubic ft of air every minute.","do":["set m view=room xray=0 speed=0.3 mt=2 hi=blades,roomAir labels=blades,roomAir"]}]}

name: centrifugal-3d
desc: 3D working model: centrifugal pump, water pump, impeller, volute, priming, pump head, shutoff head, suction lift, atmospheric pressure, affinity laws, pressure and flow, lifting water, well and tank. views: whole pump side bottom tall. parts: motor (Motor), shaft (Shaft), impeller (Impeller), eye (Inlet eye), volute (Volute (spiral casing)), outlet (Outlet), suctionPipe (Suction pipe), footValve (Foot valve), primePlug (Priming plug), riser (Pipe up), tank (Tank), water (Water). effects: cut xray. clock: slow motion, fixed windows, jump with mt: run 0-30, dry (air-filled) 30-50 at speed by 32, prime 50-70 (plug out 50-52, pouring 52-66, plug in 67-69), catch 70-90 (motor on 70-72, water climbs 72-84), climb 90-120 (tank rises 94-114), stall 120-135, faster 135-170 (3,450 to 4,140 rpm over 137-143), compare 170-200 (tank back down 171-179). At 3,450 rpm the impeller shows 0.6 turns per model second. shows: the volute with its front removed: spinning backward-curved impeller, widening spiral channel, water dots from the eye to the outlet; suction pipe from the pit through the foot valve, along the shaft into the eye; motor shell fading to show the rotor and shaft; a dry pump: air whirling, no flow, water stays in the pit; priming: plug out, water poured in, pipe filling from the foot valve up, air gone, plug in; water catching and climbing the pipe to the tank; the tank rising up a height pole until flow falls to zero at the limit marker; faster impeller: limit marker moves up, flow returns, power rises. readouts: speed (rpm), flow (gal/min), lift (ft), height limit (ft), power (hp), impeller edge speed (mph), water speed in the pipe (mph), outlet and eye pressure (psi), air's most push (ft), dry pull (in), pump filled (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: shaft seal, wear ring, check valve, pressure gauge, float switch, strainer, capacitor, gate valve, bearing, shroud, self-priming, cavitation, drive belt. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=centrifugal"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Spin water, and it climbs. This pump lifts water 40 ft, from a pit to a tank, at 54 gallons a minute. It does it with one spinning wheel. Everything is slowed way down here.","do":["set m view=whole speed=0.5 mt=0 labels=motor,tank,riser"]},{"say":"Step 2: The motor turns a shaft. Inside the motor, a rotor spins at 3,450 rpm. A steel shaft carries that spin straight into the pump, where the water is.","do":["set m view=side xray=0.9 speed=0.5 hi=motor,shaft labels=motor,shaft"]},{"say":"Step 3: The wheel throws water out. The shaft spins the impeller. Its curved vanes throw water outward, like mud off a bike tire. At the edge the wheel moves at 51 mph.","do":["set m view=pump cut=1 xray=0 speed=0.5 hi=impeller labels=impeller"]},{"say":"Step 4: The middle goes low. Water leaving the center leaves low pressure at the eye, 5 psi below the air outside. Air pressing on the pit pushes new water up the pipe to fill that gap.","do":["set m view=pump speed=0.5 hi=eye,suctionPipe labels=eye,suctionPipe"]},{"say":"Step 5: The spiral slows it down. The casing gets wider around the loop, so the fast water slows to 4 mph. Its speed turns into pressure: 16 psi at the outlet. That pressure is the push up the pipe.","do":["set m view=pump speed=0.5 hi=volute,outlet labels=volute,outlet"]},{"say":"Step 6: Up and into the tank. The steady spin keeps pulling water in at the middle and pushing it out at the edge: 54 gallons a minute, 40 ft up, for 1.1 hp.","do":["set m view=whole speed=0.5 hi=riser,tank labels=riser,tank"]}]}

name: clock-3d
desc: 3D working model: mechanical clock, pendulum clock, tall case clock, escapement, anchor escapement, escape wheel, why a clock ticks, gear train, gear ratio, second hand, minute hand, hour hand, seconds pendulum, keeping time, falling weight, pinion. views: clock dial train escapement rear. parts: weight (Falling weight), greatWheel (Great wheel and barrel), centerWheel (Center wheel (minute hand)), thirdWheel (Third wheel), escapeWheel (Escape wheel (second hand)), anchor (Anchor), crutch (Crutch), pendulum (Pendulum), secondHand (Second hand), minuteHand (Minute hand), hourHand (Hour hand), motionWork (Hour gears). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second, one tick on each whole second (even seconds entry pallet, odd exit); speed 10 is the fastest that reads. shows: a 0.994 m pendulum: round trip 2.00 s, one beat 1.00 s, swing ±3.5° over a degree scale; a 6 kg weight over a pulley falling 1.0 m in 8 days, against a height scale; great wheel 96 → 8, center wheel 64 → 8, third wheel 60 → 8: 720 : 1 from barrel to escape wheel, all teeth meshing; a 30-tooth escape wheel and anchor: the wheel locked dead still, the tooth pushing along a pallet's slanted face, the free fall that makes the tick; the contact is real geometry, 6° each beat; the crutch carrying the pendulum's swing to the anchor and the anchor's small push back; second hand on the escape arbor (60 s a turn), minute hand on the center arbor (3,600 s), hour hand through 12 → 36 and 6 → 24 (43,200 s); a live clock reading on the numbers panel. readouts: pendulum length (m), round trip and beat (s), swing and lift (°), 1 mm longer loses (s/day), weight (kg), fall (m/day, m), run (days), energy per beat (µJ), teeth and each pair's ratio, hand turn times (s), live clock time. not in the model, never say it is shown: strike, chime, bell, winding key, ratchet, click, mainspring, balance wheel, hairspring, cuckoo, moon dial, date, alarm, battery, quartz, case door, hood. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=clock"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A steady swing sets the time. The timekeeper is the pendulum. At 0.994 m long, one round trip takes 2.00 s. So each one-way swing, one beat, is 1.00 s.","do":["set m view=clock speed=1 mt=20 hi=pendulum labels=pendulum"]},{"say":"Step 2: A falling weight is the fuel. A swing dies out on its own, so the clock needs energy. A 6 kg weight falls just 0.126 m a day, and 1.0 m lasts 8 days.","do":["set m hi=weight labels=weight"]},{"say":"Step 3: Gears carry the push up. The weight turns the great wheel. Three pairs of gears, 12, 8 and 7.5 to 1, speed it up 720 times on the way to the top.","do":["set m view=train xray=0.95 hi=greatWheel,centerWheel,thirdWheel labels=greatWheel,centerWheel,thirdWheel"]},{"say":"Step 4: A gate lets it out in steps. The anchor rocks with the pendulum and stops the 30-tooth wheel, letting it jump 6° each beat. 60 beats make one turn: 60 s.","do":["set m view=escapement hi=escapeWheel labels=escapeWheel,anchor"]},{"say":"Step 5: The hands count the beats. The second hand rides on that wheel. More gears turn the minute hand once in 3,600 s and the hour hand once in 43,200 s.","do":["set m view=dial xray=0 hi=secondHand,minuteHand,hourHand labels=secondHand,minuteHand,hourHand"]},{"say":"Step 6: A nut keeps it honest. Length sets the time. Just 1 mm too long and the clock loses 43 s a day, so a small nut under the bob sets the length.","do":["set m view=clock hi=pendulum labels=pendulum"]}]}

name: clutch-3d
desc: 3D working model: clutch, friction clutch, manual transmission, stick shift, clutch pedal, stalling, stall, slipping, riding the clutch, burning clutch, friction, torque, heat from friction, flywheel, pressure plate, diaphragm spring, throwout bearing, momentum, moment of inertia. views: whole apart section gap pedal. parts: flywheel (Flywheel (on the engine)), disc (Clutch disc), facing (Friction facing), pressurePlate (Pressure plate), diaphragm (Diaphragm spring), cover (Clutch cover), bearing (Throwout bearing), fork (Clutch fork), linkage (Clutch cable), pedal (Clutch pedal), inputShaft (Input shaft (to the transmission)), housing (Bell housing). effects: cut explode. clock: 16× slow motion; fixed windows, jump with mt: pedal up on a 10 % hill 0-10, pedal pressed and braking 10-30, stopped with pedal down 30-40, smooth start 40-72, pedal dropped (stall) 72-92, riding the clutch 92-124 (heat clock runs fast: 3.75 s of crawling per model s, 120 s in all). shows: flywheel, disc, pressure plate, diaphragm spring and cover in section and spread apart along the shaft; engine-side parts gray and tan, transmission-side parts blue; pedal → cable → fork → throwout bearing → finger tips → spring tips over its pivot → plate lifts; all travel drawn 5 × bigger than life, readouts give real sizes (pedal 5.5 in, bearing 0.31 in, plate 0.06 in); clamp 1,000 lb lets the clutch hold 164 lb-ft against the engine's 110 lb-ft top; foot force 16 lb; white bars on the flywheel and dark bars on the disc show one piece or slipping; live rpm of each; smooth start: engine held at 1,500 rpm, disc catches up from rest in about 1.6 s, about 14 hp of heat at the peak; stall: pedal dropped at idle 800 rpm, disc grabs, engine falls under 400 rpm and stops; car rolls 1 mph and halts. The car feels 3 × the engine's spin inertia, so a sudden grab leaves about 200 rpm; riding: crawling up a 10 % hill with the pedal 41 % down: engine 1,800 rpm, disc 200 rpm, 6.8 of 7.7 hp becomes heat, facing goes from 180 °F past the 480 °F limit to about 590 °F in 120 s, same heat as about 79 smooth starts; facing scorches in color. readouts: pedal down (%), clamp (lb), clutch can hold (lb-ft), engine can give (lb-ft), engine and disc speed (rpm), slip (rpm), car speed (mph), torque passed (lb-ft), heat (hp), facing temp (°F), time (s), same heat as (starts), foot force (lb), pedal, bearing, plate travel (in). not in the model, never say it is shown: master cylinder, slave cylinder, clutch fluid, pilot bearing, starter motor, retract strap, cushion spring, dual-mass flywheel, synchro, shift lever, gas pedal, brake pedal, dust. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=clutch"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A switch for the engine. An engine never stops turning, but a car has to stop at red lights. The clutch connects the engine to the wheels, or lets go of them.","do":["set m view=whole speed=1 mt=2 labels=housing,linkage"]},{"say":"Step 2: It is a sandwich. The clutch disc sits between two parts that always turn with the engine: the flywheel and the pressure plate. The disc turns the shaft that goes to the wheels.","do":["set m view=apart explode=1 speed=0.5 hi=disc labels=flywheel,disc,pressurePlate,diaphragm,cover"]},{"say":"Step 3: Pedal up: squeezed tight. A big spring presses the plate with 1,000 lb. Friction then lets the disc hold 164 lb-ft, more than the engine's 111. Nothing slips: all at 2,000 rpm.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 explode=0 speed=1 mt=5 hi=diaphragm,pressurePlate labels=diaphragm,pressurePlate,facing,inputShaft"]},{"say":"Step 4: Press the pedal. Your foot pushes with 16 lb. A cable pulls a lever called the fork, and the fork shoves a bearing 0.31 in against the spring's fingers.","do":["set m view=pedal speed=1 mt=11 hi=pedal,fork,linkage,bearing labels=pedal,linkage,fork,bearing"]},{"say":"Step 5: The squeeze lets go. The fingers go in, so the spring's outer edge lifts the plate 0.06 in. Clamp drops to 0 lb. (All this movement is drawn 5 times bigger so you can see it.)","do":["set m view=gap speed=0.2 mt=21 hi=pedal,diaphragm,pressurePlate labels=diaphragm,pressurePlate,facing"]},{"say":"Step 6: Engine runs, car stops. Now the engine turns freely at 800 rpm while the disc stands at 0, and so does the car. You can change gears with no twist on them.","do":["set m view=section speed=1 mt=32 hi= labels=flywheel,disc"]},{"say":"Step 7: Pedal up slowly. Lift your foot and the plate squeezes again. At first the facing slips, so the disc speeds up gently. Soon it matches the engine's 1,500 rpm and they lock as one.","do":["set m view=section speed=3 mt=46 hi=facing labels=facing,disc"]}]}

name: coaster-3d
desc: 3D working model: roller coaster, energy conversion, potential energy, kinetic energy, conservation of energy, friction, g-force, loop, circular motion, centripetal force. views: full climb loop top end. parts: liftHill (Lift hill and chain), firstDrop (First drop), secondHill (Second hill), loop (Loop), thirdHill (Third hill), brakeRun (Brake run), train (Train), rider (Rider), lapBar (Lap bar), wheels (Wheels above and below the rail), forces (Gravity (blue), seat push (orange)), energyLine (Highest it can still reach). effects: none. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second of the ride; t = 0 at the foot of the lift, train stops at about 51.4. shows: a chain hauling the train up a 40 m lift hill at 3 m/s; potential energy turning into kinetic energy and back, on every hill, with a stacked energy bar; speed, height, potential, kinetic, energy lost as heat and g-force on a rider, all at any moment; the top of a teardrop loop: gravity and seat-push arrows on a rider, speed needed versus speed had; a falling line showing the highest the train could still reach, against 40 m, 30 m, 24 m and 18 m hills; wheels above and below the rail, lap bars, brake calipers squeezing a fin. readouts: speed (m/s), height (m), potential energy (kJ), kinetic energy (kJ), energy lost as heat (kJ), g-force (g), speed needed at the loop top (m/s), loop top radius (m), highest it can still reach (m). not in the model, never say it is shown: launch, catapult, station, corkscrew, banked turn, banking, transfer track, anti-rollback, harness, seat belt, headrest, block section, magnetic brake, queue. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=coaster"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: One chain does the lifting. A motor pulls a chain that drags the train up the first hill at a steady 3 m/s. That is the last push the train gets for the whole ride.","do":["set m view=climb speed=2.7 mt=5.9 hi=liftHill labels=liftHill,train"]},{"say":"Step 2: Energy stored in height. At the top, 40 m up, the train holds 1,960 kJ of potential energy: energy saved up by being high. It is barely moving, so its kinetic energy, the energy of motion, is only 20 kJ.","do":["set m speed=1.32 hi=train labels=train"]},{"say":"Step 3: Falling turns height into speed. At the bottom, potential is down to 150 kJ and kinetic is up to 1,730 kJ. The train hits 26 m/s, about 59 mph, with nothing pushing it. A rider feels 3.4 g in the seat.","do":["set m speed=0.5 hi=firstDrop labels=firstDrop"]},{"say":"Step 4: Speed climbs the next hill. No chain here. Its speed carries it up to 30 m, and the energy swaps back: kinetic falls to 330 kJ, potential climbs to 1,470 kJ. Riders feel light, just 0.5 g.","do":["set m speed=0.5 hi=secondHill labels=secondHill"]},{"say":"Step 5: The same swap, again and again. Down makes speed, up makes height. Nothing pushes it, even in the loop. At the top, 1,200 kJ is stored and 400 kJ is moving it at 13 m/s.","do":["set m view=loop speed=1.32 hi=loop labels=loop"]},{"say":"Step 6: Brakes spend what is left. Friction took some energy all along. Now brakes squeeze a fin under the train and turn its motion into heat. The whole ride ran on that one trip up the chain.","do":["set m view=end speed=1 hi=brakeRun labels=brakeRun"]}]}

name: collision-3d
desc: 3D working model: momentum, conservation of momentum, collision, elastic collision, inelastic collision, impulse, force and time, Newton's third law, kinetic energy, dynamics cart, crumple zone, seat belt, airbag, car crash, crash test. views: track contact bars crash cabin. parts: cartA (Cart A), cartB (Cart B), spring (Spring bumper), pad (Sticky pad), momentumBars (Momentum bars), energyBars (Energy bars), forces (Equal and opposite pushes), crumple (Crumple zone), stiffCar (Stiff front end), belt (Seat belt), airbag (Airbag), figure (Crash-test figure). effects: xray. clock: model seconds are real seconds. 0-10 spring bumper 2+2 kg, 10-20 sticky pad 2+2 kg, 20-30 spring bumper 2+6 kg, 30-40 sticky pad 2+6 kg: cart A at 1.0 m/s touches at 0.8 s after the window starts, the run holds when a cart reaches an end stop. 200-220 crumple car against stiff car, barrier at t 200.30. 220-240 belted car against unbelted car, barrier at t 220.30. Jump with mt; use speed 0 to hold, about 0.015 for the crash. shows: a 2.0 kg cart at 1.0 m/s hitting a 2.0 kg cart or a 6.0 kg cart at rest, total momentum 2.0 kg·m/s at every instant; momentum bars for A, B and the total; A's bar goes negative when it bounces back; energy bars: the spring bumper keeps 1.00 J, the sticky pad leaves 0.50 J (2+2 kg) or 0.25 J (2+6 kg); equal and opposite push arrows to scale while the carts touch, 0.20 s and 16 N peak with the spring; two cars at 35 mph (15.6 m/s) hitting a barrier side by side, front folding: 0.70 m of crush against 0.10 m; car stop: 0.089 s and 262,000 N with a crumple zone, 0.013 s and 1,840,000 N stiff; same 23,500 kg·m/s; a 75 kg crash-test figure, belt and airbag: 0.128 s and 9,180 N in the crumple car, 0.051 s and 23,000 N in the stiff car; the same figure with no belt and no airbag reaching the dashboard at 12.5 m/s: 0.008 s and 118,000 N; a force against time board: tall and thin or low and long, drawn as the crash runs; the near side and roof of each car fade under x-ray to show the figure. readouts: mass (kg), speed (m/s), momentum (kg·m/s), energy (J), push (N), touching time (s), impulse (N·s), stop time (s), force (N). not in the model, never say it is shown: air track, photogate, ball, engine, brake, tire, passenger, child seat, head restraint, side impact, truck, motorcycle, rebound. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=collision"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Momentum is mass times velocity. Velocity is speed with a direction. Cart A is 2.0 kg rolling at 1.00 m/s, so its momentum is 2.0 kg·m/s. Cart B is sitting still, so its momentum is 0.","do":["set m view=track speed=0.1 mt=0 labels=cartA,cartB,momentumBars"]},{"say":"Step 2: Each cart pushes the other. While they touch, A pushes B exactly as hard as B pushes A, for the same 0.20 s. Each push is an impulse of 2.0 N·s.","do":["set m view=contact speed=0.045 mt=0.76 hi=forces labels=forces,spring"]},{"say":"Step 3: One loses what the other gains. Halfway through the bump, A has 1.0 kg·m/s and B has 1.0 kg·m/s. A's loss is B's gain, so the total is still 2.0.","do":["set m view=bars speed=0 mt=0.8993 hi=momentumBars labels=momentumBars"]},{"say":"Step 4: The momentum moved across. After the bump, A has stopped and B rolls at 1.00 m/s. All 2.0 kg·m/s now belongs to B.","do":["set m view=track speed=0.15 mt=1 hi=momentumBars labels=cartA,cartB"]},{"say":"Step 5: Try a heavier cart. Now B is 6.0 kg. A bounces back at 0.50 m/s, which counts as -1.0 kg·m/s, and B takes 3.0. Add them up: still 2.0.","do":["set m view=track speed=0.2 mt=20.7 hi=momentumBars labels=cartA,cartB"]},{"say":"Step 6: Only an outside push changes it. The carts' pushes on each other always cancel. The track has very low friction, so nothing outside changes the total of 2.0 kg·m/s.","do":["set m view=bars speed=0 labels=momentumBars"]}]}

desc: 3D working model: pressure cooker, boiling point, boiling and pressure, vapor pressure, altitude cooking, high altitude, Denver, air pressure, atmospheric pressure, steam, phase change, safety valve, pressure regulator, gasket, kitchen science. views: hero section lid compare mountain. parts: pot (Pot), gasket (Rubber gasket), lidLock (Lid lock (tabs and pin)), regulator (Pressure regulator), backupValve (Backup safety valve), water (Water), steam (Trapped steam), thermometer (Thermometer), gauge (Pressure dial), seaPot (Open pot at sea level), denverPot (Open pot in Denver), air (Air above the pot). effects: cut. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt. Safety 110-170: normal 110-120, regulator blocked 120-128, backup open at 20 psi 128-138, backup blocked 138-146, gasket lets go at 30 psi 146-150, heat off and pressure falls 150-158, pin drops 158, lid opens 160-168. Only the things of that window are on show: cook = cooker + left pot, pots = two open pots with their air, safety = cooker. shows: home stovetop pressure cooker cut open: pot, lid, rubber gasket, steel tabs, lock pin, regulator weight on its vent, backup valve, water, beans, steam dots that crowd together as pressure rises; dial thermometer and pressure dial on the lid, reading the same numbers as the panel; live chart of boiling point against total pressure, with marks for Denver, sea level and the cooker and a dot that moves; an open pot beside the cooker, boiling at 212 °F; two open pots under columns of air: the right pot rises to Denver height, its air column gets shorter, its water drops to 202 °F; safety layers in order, each opening with soft steam: regulator at 15 psi, backup valve at 20, gasket through a slot in the lid at 30; a bean blocks each vent; heat off, pressure falls to 0, lock pin drops, lid turns and lifts. readouts: water temperature (°F), pressure above outside air (psi), total pressure on the water (psi), air push at sea level and Denver (psi), altitude (ft), minutes to cook beans, push on the lid (lb), valve opening pressures (psi). not in the model, never say it is shown: timer, rack, trivet, basket, electric cooker, pressure sensor, control panel, float valve, whistle, release lever, thermostat, inner pot. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=cooker"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A pot with a sealed lid. A rubber gasket seals the lid and steel tabs hold it on. Now the steam from the boiling water has nowhere to go.","do":["set m view=hero speed=1.6 mt=0 hi= labels=pot,gasket,lidLock"]},{"say":"Step 2: Water hits 212 °F. With the pressure still at 0, the water reaches 212 °F. In an open pot it stays stuck there, because extra heat just makes steam.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 speed=0.8 mt=8 hi=water labels=water,thermometer"]},{"say":"Step 3: Steam piles up. Here the steam stays trapped, so more and more of it crowds into the same space. Watch the pressure dial and the chart climb.","do":["set m view=section speed=1.8 mt=11 hi=steam labels=steam,gauge"]},{"say":"Step 4: Pressure raises the boiling point. The cooker adds 15 psi to the 14.7 psi of normal air, 29.7 psi in total. Under that squeeze, water does not boil until 250 °F.","do":["set m view=lid speed=1 mt=24 hi=gauge,thermometer labels=gauge,thermometer"]},{"say":"Step 5: Hotter water, faster food. Food cooks about twice as fast for every 18 °F hotter. So beans that take 120 minutes in the open pot at 212 °F take about 30 in the cooker.","do":["set m view=compare speed=1 mt=31 hi=seaPot labels=seaPot,pot"]}]}

name: cooling-3d
desc: 3D working model: car cooling system, engine cooling, radiator, water pump, thermostat, coolant, antifreeze, overheating, radiator cap, pressure and boiling point, boiling point, water jacket, heat transfer, engine warm-up. views: bay engine thermostat radiator cap. parts: block (Engine block), jacket (Water jacket), pump (Water pump), thermostat (Thermostat), bypass (Bypass hose), upperHose (Upper hose), lowerHose (Lower hose), radiator (Radiator), fan (Fan), cap (Pressure cap), tank (Overflow tank), coolant (Coolant). effects: cut xray. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: warm-up 0-40 (cold until 9, thermostat opens near 25), running 40-70, fan quits 70-110 (boils near 90), thermostat stuck shut 110-140 (boils near 128), hot cap 140-165 (opened at 148), cooling down with cap on 165-180. Real minutes pass in the window's own map; speed 1 reads well. shows: the whole loop: pump, water jacket around the cylinders, thermostat, upper hose, radiator tubes, lower hose, back to the pump; coolant dots colored by temperature: blue cold, amber hot, red boiling hot; white bubbles in the jacket when boiling; thermostat with its wax pellet, spring and valve sliding open; bypass carrying the flow while it is shut; air through the radiator, blue in, warmer out, only while the fan runs; overflow tank level rising as the coolant grows and when it boils; two ways to overheat: fan quits in traffic, thermostat stuck shut with a cold radiator; opening a hot cap: pressure drops, boiling point falls below the coolant's temperature, steam and hot spray burst out; cooling down with the cap on, time to 140 °F. readouts: coolant temperature (°F), thermostat % open, pressure (psi), boiling point (°F), pump flow, radiator flow, bypass flow (gal/min), engine rpm, heat from engine and heat leaving (hp), radiator in and out (°F), outside air (°F), oil thickness compared with hot oil, coolant in the tank (gal), minutes since start, since fan quit, engine off. not in the model, never say it is shown: heater core, head gasket, hose clamp, temperature sensor, oil pump, crankshaft, transmission cooler, drain plug, alternator, condenser, turbo, air conditioner. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=cooling"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Carry the heat away. Burning gas makes far more heat than the car can use. On this 85 °F day about 27 hp of it goes into the coolant, which is water mixed with antifreeze.","do":["set m view=bay speed=1 mt=40 labels=block,fan"]},{"say":"Step 2: Around the cylinders. A belt spins the water pump, pushing 20 gallons a minute through the water jacket, channels around the cylinders. Coolant goes in at 196 °F and leaves at 203 °F.","do":["set m view=engine cut=1 speed=1 hi=jacket,pump labels=jacket,pump"]},{"say":"Step 3: Through the gate. The thermostat sits at the top like a gate. Right now it is 38% open, so about 8 gallons a minute go on to the radiator and the rest takes the bypass back.","do":["set m view=thermostat cut=0 speed=1 hi=thermostat,upperHose labels=thermostat,bypass,upperHose"]},{"say":"Step 4: Dump it in the air. Hot coolant trickles down many thin tubes with fins, and the fan pulls air past them. It comes in at 203 °F and leaves at 184 °F. About 24 hp of heat leaves here.","do":["set m view=radiator speed=1 hi=radiator,fan labels=radiator,fan"]},{"say":"Step 5: Sealed and squeezed. The lower hose takes the cooled coolant back to the pump. The cap keeps the loop at 15 psi, so coolant boils at 265 °F, not 223 °F. The tank catches any that it pushes out.","do":["set m view=cap speed=1 mt=60 hi=cap,tank labels=cap,tank,lowerHose"]}]}

name: cvt-3d
desc: 3D working model: CVT, continuously variable transmission, automatic transmission, pulley, belt drive, steel belt, gear ratio, engine speed, engine sound, rpm, torque, scooter, snowmobile, moped, variator, flyweights, centrifugal force, centrifugal clutch, wedge, ramp. views: whole ratio section board scooter weights wedge rear spring. parts: engine (Engine), pulleyIn (Input pulley), pulleyOut (Output pulley), sliding (Sliding half), belt (Steel belt), wheel (Wheel (drawn small)), frontSlide (Sliding half), rollers (Flyweights), ramp (Ramp plate), rubberBelt (Rubber belt), spring (Rear spring), shoes (Clutch shoes). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 second of driving; parts drawn turning 100 × slower than real. Jump with mt: car at steady 2,000 rpm 0-30 (ratio low until 10, sweeps to top by 26), car pedal down 30-52 (4,000 rpm reached at 32, held to 65 mph at 39.5, eases to cruise by 45.5), scooter 100-140 (idle until 104, clutch bites 105-108, weights start 111, fully out 127, throttle closed 132). shows: car: two pulleys, each two cones, with a steel block belt between; one cone of each slides on oil, belt radius follows from the cone angle and the fixed belt length; ratio 2.50 to 0.42 at steady 2,000 rpm: wheels 150 to 880 rpm, 11 to 66 mph, torque at wheels 668 to 112 lb-ft; section through the shafts shows the V gap closing and the belt lifting; x-ray turns the near cones to glass so the belt can be seen riding up and down; pedal down: engine climbs to 4,000 rpm then holds while the car goes 22 to 65 mph and the ratio falls 2.50 to 0.85, with a board: tach, speedometer and engine vs speed chart against a six-gear car's sawtooth; belt squeeze (lb) and oil pressure (psi) when the sliding half is highlighted; scooter: six 0.4 oz flyweights on a curved ramp push the sliding half; rear spring pushes back; balance sets engine speed 4,730-6,210 rpm and ratio 2.40-0.72, 12-51 mph; scooter clutch: three shoes bite the bell at 3,600 engine rpm (seen from the far side), gap drawn bigger than life; car's and scooter's wheels are drawn small; belt has fewer, bigger blocks than real. readouts: engine (rpm), ratio, pulley, wheel speed (rpm), car, scooter speed (mph), torque at wheels (lb-ft), engine power (hp), fixed-gear car engine (rpm), belt circle diameters (in), belt squeeze (lb), oil pressure (psi), weight pull and push (lb), spring (lb), shoe fling (lb), one weight (oz). not in the model, never say it is shown: torque converter, oil pump, valve body, transmission computer, planetary gear, reverse gear, differential, torque cam, kill switch, drive chain, starter. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=cvt"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A box with no gear steps. This box sits between the engine and the wheels. A CVT does not click through 1st, 2nd and 3rd. It has no gears to choose from, only one fixed pair on the way to the wheels.","do":["set m view=whole xray=0 speed=1 mt=0 labels=engine,wheel"]},{"say":"Step 2: Two pulleys and a steel belt. The engine turns the input pulley. A belt of steel blocks carries that turning across to the output pulley, and on to the wheels.","do":["set m view=whole xray=1 speed=1 hi=belt labels=pulleyIn,pulleyOut,belt"]},{"say":"Step 3: Each pulley is two cones. Here it is sliced open: two cones face each other with the belt between. Oil pushes one cone in, so the belt gets squeezed outward to a bigger circle. Let it back and the belt sinks.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 xray=0 speed=1 mt=10 hi=sliding labels=sliding,belt"]},{"say":"Step 4: Low: small circle turns big. To start off, the belt rides low on the input and high on the output. The ratio is 2.50: the engine at 2,000 rpm turns the wheels only 150 rpm. Slow, but 668 lb-ft of push.","do":["set m view=ratio cut=0 xray=1 speed=1 mt=0 hi= labels=pulleyIn,pulleyOut"]},{"say":"Step 5: It slides, it never clicks. The belt can't stretch, so as it climbs one pulley it sinks on the other. The ratio passes smoothly through every value. Here it is 1.00: both pulleys at 2,000 rpm.","do":["set m view=ratio speed=1 mt=15.55 hi=belt labels=belt"]},{"say":"Step 6: High: big circle turns small. Now the ratio is 0.42. The same 2,000 rpm engine spins the wheels 880 rpm, so the car does 66 mph. Less push, 112 lb-ft, but far more speed.","do":["set m view=ratio speed=0.6 mt=26 hi= labels=pulleyIn,pulleyOut"]}]}

name: diesel-3d
desc: 3D working model: diesel engine, compression ignition, no spark plugs, glow plug, fuel injector, direct injection, gas vs diesel, why trucks use diesel, torque, pickup truck engine, inline-6. views: block section chamber compare compareTop. parts: block (Engine block), piston (Piston with bowl), rod (Connecting rod), crank (Crankshaft), intakeValve (Intake valve), exhaustValve (Exhaust valve), injector (Fuel injector), glowPlug (Glow plug), air (Inside the cylinder), spray (Fuel spray), gasEngine (Gas engine, same size), turbo (Turbo). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = half a crank turn (180°); one full cycle = 4 s. shows: intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes with valve timing, air only until the fuel arrives; air heated by squeezing to about 1,200 °F at 17.3:1, the fuel spraying in at 29,000 psi and lighting itself just after the top; bowl in the piston crown, and the 1 mm gap left above the rim; glow plug heating for cold starts (tip glows when glowPlug is highlighted); highlight gasEngine: a gas cylinder of the same size appears beside it at 10:1 with spark plug, running in step; the panel compares both; highlight crank: the panel shows torque and power ratings; crank plus gasEngine compares ratings and fuel use; x-ray: all six pistons in firing order 1-5-3-6-2-4. readouts: stroke name, squeeze ratio, cylinder pressure (psi), temperature (°F), fuel spray pressure (psi), piston push (lb), fuel lighting point (°F), glow plug heat (°F), torque (lb-ft), power (hp), rpm, efficiency, share of fuel energy turned into motion (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: timing chain, timing belt, belt, flywheel, transmission, clutch, radiator, water pump, oil pump, fuel pump, fuel tank, fuel filter, air filter, intercooler, starter, alternator, exhaust filter, muffler. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=diesel"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Six cylinders, no spark plugs. This truck engine has 6 cylinders and not one spark plug. So what lights the fuel? Let's cut one cylinder open.","do":["set m view=block speed=0.5 mt=0 labels=block,injector"]},{"say":"Step 2: Air goes in, only air. The piston slides down and pulls in air, with no fuel at all. Then the valves shut and the piston starts back up.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 speed=0.24 mt=0.3 hi=air labels=intakeValve,air,piston"]},{"say":"Step 3: Squeezing makes it hot. Squeeze a gas hard and it heats up, like a bike pump getting warm. Here the air is already at 1,380 psi and 1,130 °F.","do":["set m view=chamber speed=0.0093 mt=1.9222 hi=air labels=air,piston"]},{"say":"Step 4: Fuel sprays in. At the very top the injector sprays a fine mist at 29,000 psi. The air is at 1,200 °F. Diesel fuel lights at just 410 °F.","do":["set m speed=0.0074 mt=1.9778 hi=injector,spray labels=injector,spray"]},{"say":"Step 5: It lights itself. No spark is needed. The fuel catches fire on its own, and the pressure jumps to 2,290 psi. That shoves the piston down with 31,730 lb and turns the crankshaft.","do":["set m speed=0.0222 mt=2.0222 hi=air labels=piston,air"]},{"say":"Step 6: Cold mornings. A freezing engine soaks up that heat. So a glow plug heats to 1,800 °F for a few seconds to warm the air. It is a heater, not a spark, and it rests once the engine runs.","do":["set m view=chamber speed=0.2 mt=0.2 hi=glowPlug labels=glowPlug"]}]}

name: differential-3d
desc: 3D working model: differential, open differential, rear axle, final drive, ring and pinion, ring gear, bevel gears, spider gears, cornering, wheel speed, car axle. views: axle diff spiders ringPinion top. parts: driveShaft (Drive shaft), pinion (Pinion gear), ringGear (Ring gear), carrier (Carrier), spiderGears (Spider gears), sideGears (Side gears), halfShafts (Axle shafts), leftWheel (Left wheel), rightWheel (Right wheel), housing (Axle housing), outerPath (Outer wheel path), innerPath (Inner wheel path). effects: cut xray. clock: 10× slow motion; fixed windows, jump with mt: straight 0-12, right turn, radius 16 ft, 12-40 (eases in over 12-14, out over 40-42), straight 42-52. shows: drive shaft and pinion (11 teeth) driving the ring gear (41 teeth): final drive 3.73 : 1, 574 rpm in, 154 rpm out; carrier bolted to the ring, carrying two spider gears on a cross pin; two side gears splined to the axle shafts; straight at 11 mph: spiders still on their pin, both wheels 154 rpm; right turn, 16 ft radius: inner wheel 131 rpm, outer 177 rpm, carrier 154 rpm (the average), spiders spin at 37 rpm; seen from above: car outline, front wheels steered, both rear wheel paths over a quarter turn (outer 30 ft, inner 22 ft); torque: 13 lb-ft into the pinion, 49 lb-ft out of the ring (× 3.73), split 24.5 lb-ft to each axle, equal on the corner while the speeds differ; bevel teeth meshing on cones (checked: they never pass through each other). readouts: drive shaft rpm, carrier rpm, left / right wheel rpm, turn radius (ft), final drive ratio, spider spin rpm, pinion / ring teeth, outer / inner wheel path (ft), car speed (mph), pinion / ring torque (lb-ft), left / right axle torque (lb-ft). not in the model, never say it is shown: limited-slip, locking differential, clutch pack, hypoid offset, bearing, oil, transmission, engine, brake, suspension, front differential, four-wheel drive, universal joint. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=differential"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Going straight. Driving straight, both back wheels roll the same distance in the same time. So they turn at the same speed: 154 rpm each.","do":["set m view=top speed=1 mt=2"]},{"say":"Step 2: Two circles, two sizes. In a turn each wheel follows its own circle. The outer circle is bigger: over a quarter turn the outer wheel travels 30 ft, the inner wheel only 22 ft.","do":["set m mt=15 hi=outerPath,innerPath labels=outerPath,innerPath"]},{"say":"Step 3: Same time, more distance. Both wheels get around the corner together. To cover more ground in the same time, the outer wheel must spin faster: 177 rpm against 131 rpm.","do":["set m hi=outerPath labels=outerPath,innerPath"]},{"say":"Step 4: Locked together, a tire would skid. If both wheels were stuck at one speed, one tire would have to slide and scrub on the road. The car would push wide and the tires would wear out.","do":["set m view=axle hi=leftWheel,rightWheel labels=leftWheel,rightWheel"]},{"say":"Step 5: The differential fixes this. In the middle of the axle, small spider gears start to spin, at 37 rpm. That lets the outer wheel run ahead of the inner one, while the drive shaft still drives both.","do":["set m view=diff cut=1 speed=1.5 mt=22 hi=spiderGears labels=spiderGears,sideGears"]}]}

name: drone-3d
desc: 3D working model: drone, quadcopter, propeller, thrust, hover, weight, downwash, torque, yaw, tilt, Newton's third law, flight controller, forward flight. views: threeq side top inside wide. parts: frame (Body and arms), motors (Motors), propsCW (Clockwise props), propsCCW (Counterclockwise props), controller (Flight controller), battery (Battery), gimbal (Camera gimbal), legs (Landing legs), downwash (Air pushed down), thrust (Thrust), weight (Weight), twist (Twist on the body). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second (slow it with speed; props are drawn at 1/40 of their real rate); fixed windows, jump with mt: lift-off and hover 0-12, climb 12-24, forward flight 24-40, yaw turn 40-52, what if all four spun the same way 52-60. shows: four props on an X frame, diagonal pairs spinning the same way, color-coded (blue clockwise, purple counterclockwise); idle 1,910 rpm on the ground, spin-up, lift-off at up to 113% of weight, hover at 4,920 rpm with thrust = weight; a thrust arrow on each prop sized by its thrust; the weight arrow; air pushed down through each prop (23 mph below it in a hover), spreading on the ground, swept back in forward flight; climb at 7 mph up to 66 ft: 5,450 rpm on every motor, thrust still 100% of weight; forward flight: back pair faster (~5,300 vs ~4,500 rpm) tips the nose down, the tilted thrust speeds it up, cruise at 22 mph and 15° tilt; yaw: each prop twists the body the opposite way (6.4 oz-in), twists cancel in a hover; clockwise pair faster turns it left 90° in place; what if all four spun the same way (53-53.3): the twists add to 25.7 oz-in and the body spins the other way, up to 125 °/s; put back to two and two, the other pair brakes it (up to 5,770 vs 3,890 rpm) and it holds still 112° around; x-ray: flight controller board and battery inside the body; the gimbal keeps the camera level. readouts: four motor rpm, thrust as % of weight, height (ft), climb rate (mph), downwash speed (mph), tilt angle, speed (mph), twist left over (oz-in), turn rate (°/s), angle turned. not in the model, never say it is shown: GPS, gyroscope, accelerometer, compass, antenna, remote control, obstacle sensor, propeller guard, speed controller, LED, ground effect, gust. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=drone"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Four motors, four props. A drone has four motors, each turning a propeller. Sitting on the ground, the props idle at about 1,910 rpm.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0.3 mt=0 labels=propsCW,propsCCW,motors"]},{"say":"Step 2: Speed up to lift off. The motors speed up. Each prop gets pushed up as it throws air down: that push is thrust. When thrust beats the weight, the drone rises.","do":["set m speed=0.4 mt=1.5 hi=thrust labels=thrust"]},{"say":"Step 3: Air pushed down. Hovering, the props push air down at about 23 mph. Pushing air down pushes the drone up, the same way a swimmer pushes water back to go forward.","do":["set m view=wide speed=0.3 mt=6 hi=downwash labels=downwash"]},{"say":"Step 4: Thrust = weight. All four motors spin at 4,920 rpm. Their thrust adds up to exactly the weight, 100%, so the drone neither rises nor falls: it stays still.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.4 mt=8 hi=thrust,weight labels=thrust,weight"]},{"say":"Step 5: A tiny pilot inside. Wind and bumps keep nudging it. The flight controller feels every tilt and changes the four motor speeds many times a second to keep it level and in place.","do":["set m view=inside xray=1 speed=0.3 mt=10 hi=controller labels=controller,battery"]}]}

name: elevator-3d
desc: 3D working model: elevator, traction elevator, counterweight, sheave, pulley, steel cables, elevator brake, governor, safety brake, cable breaks, friction, balance, energy saving. views: overview middle machine governor safety. parts: car (Car), counterweight (Counterweight), cables (Six steel cables), sheave (Sheave (grooved wheel)), motor (Motor), brake (Brake), rails (Guide rails), governor (Governor), govRope (Governor rope), safety (Safety brake), buffer (Buffers). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second; one continuous story in 12 s blocks (up, down, no counterweight, balanced, full, empty, parked, cables gone). shows: car and counterweight hanging on six cables over a grooved sheave, moving in opposite directions; a normal 36 ft trip at 350 ft/min: brake opens, motor turns the sheave, grooves grip the cables, brake shuts at the floor; guide rails keeping car and counterweight straight; weight comparison with arrows: no counterweight (5,400 lb, 72 hp), 8 riders balanced (0 lb, 0 hp), full (2,100 lb, 28 hp), empty (1,400 lb, 19 hp), 99 hp full with no counterweight; one of six cables gone while the others hold; each holds 14,500 lb, 87,000 lb together, 11.6 times a full car's 7,500 lb; every cable gone: governor reaches 400 ft/min, its weights swing out, a jaw grips the governor rope, the wedges under the car clamp the rails, stop within 2.7 ft in 0.6 s. readouts: speed (ft/min), floor, height (ft), riders, car side (lb), counterweight (lb), difference (lb), motor power (hp), sheave rpm and size (in), brake open/shut, cables left, cable strength (lb), governor rpm, trip speed (ft/min), stop distance (ft), stop time (s). not in the model, never say it is shown: door, controller, button, gearbox, traveling cable, compensation chain, sensor, hydraulic, machine-room-less, regeneration. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=elevator"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Two ends of one set of cables. The car hangs on one end of six steel cables. A heavy counterweight hangs on the other end. The cables run over a grooved wheel at the top, called a sheave.","do":["set m view=overview speed=0.05 mt=0 labels=car,counterweight,cables,sheave"]},{"say":"Step 2: The brake lets go. The brake holds the machine still whenever the car is parked. To start a trip it opens. With 12 riders, the car side is 700 lb heavier than the counterweight.","do":["set m view=machine speed=0.25 mt=1.2 hi=brake labels=brake,motor,sheave"]},{"say":"Step 3: The motor turns the wheel. The motor spins the sheave at 45 rpm. Nothing winds up. The grooves grip the cables by friction and drag them along at 350 ft/min, using just 9 hp.","do":["set m speed=0.35 hi=motor,sheave labels=motor,sheave"]},{"say":"Step 4: Rails keep it straight. Shoes on the car slide along 2 guide rails, and the counterweight has 2 more. That makes 4 rails, so nothing sways or swings as it travels.","do":["set m view=middle speed=0.35 hi=rails labels=rails,car,counterweight"]},{"say":"Step 5: One goes up, one comes down. The car and the counterweight always move the same distance in opposite directions. Near the floor the motor slows down. Then the brake shuts and holds everything still.","do":["set m view=overview speed=0.4 hi=car,counterweight labels=car,counterweight"]}]}

name: ev-3d
desc: 3D working model: electric car, EV, battery pack, inverter, AC motor, regenerative braking, regen, why no gears, single-speed, reduction gear, range, kWh, torque, instant torque, DC to AC. views: hero pack drive motor wheel. parts: body (Car body), battery (Battery pack), dcCables (DC cables), inverter (Inverter), acCables (3 AC wires), motor (AC motor), stator (Coils (stator)), rotor (Magnet rotor), gears (Reduction gears), axle (Drive shafts), wheels (Drive wheels), brakes (Friction brakes). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second of the drive; spinning parts are drawn at 1/20 real speed. Holding 65 mph on the highway takes just 18 hp.","do":["set m view=hero speed=1 mt=20 labels=wheels"]},{"say":"Step 2: The battery is the floor. 16 modules hold 4,416 small cells, flat under the seats. Together they store 75 kWh at 350 volts and weigh 1,040 lb.","do":["set m view=pack xray=0.95 speed=0.4 hi=battery labels=battery"]},{"say":"Step 3: The inverter makes AC. A battery pushes current one way (DC). This motor needs current that flips (AC). The inverter swings it back and forth 490 times a second, onto 3 wires.","do":["set m view=drive cut=1 xray=0 speed=0.15 hi=inverter,acCables labels=inverter,acCables,dcCables"]},{"say":"Step 4: Coils pull magnets.
