About 87% of the battery's energy reaches the wheels. A full pack lasts about 320 miles at 65 mph.","do":["set m view=hero cut=0 speed=1 hi= labels=wheels"]}]}

name: excavator-3d
desc: 3D working model: excavator, hydraulics, hydraulic cylinder, pressure, force, pressure times area, gear pump, control valve, spool valve, joystick, lever linkage, swing motor, tracks, ground pressure, traction, construction machine. views: side cylinder hood cab ground. parts: boom (Boom), stick (Stick), bucket (Bucket), boomCylinder (Boom cylinder), stickCylinder (Stick cylinder), bucketCylinder (Bucket cylinder), gearPump (Gear pump), valves (Control valves), joystick (Joystick), swingMotor (Swing motor), tracks (Tracks), tires (Eight truck tires). effects: xray. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: dig cycle 0-40 (boom down 0-3, stick in 3-8, bucket curls 8-12, stalled at full pressure 12-16, curls 16-19, boom up 19-24, swing 24-28, dump 28-31, swing back 31-35, back to start 35-38); name: exchanger-3d
desc: 3D working model: heat exchanger, shell and tube, counter flow, parallel flow, heat transfer, surface area, fins, car radiator, baffles, effectiveness, temperature gap, thin tubes. views: side close end radiator fins. parts: shell (Shell), tubes (Tubes), baffles (Baffle), heads (End cap), hotIn (Hot water in), hotOut (Hot water out), coldIn (Cold water in), coldOut (Cold water out), wall (Tube wall), radTubes (Flat tubes (coolant)), fins (Fins), air (Air). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second, jump with mt. A heat exchanger takes heat out of one liquid and puts it into another. Here, 90 °C water warms 20 °C water at 65 kW.","do":["set m view=side cut=0 speed=1 mt=0 labels=hotIn,coldIn"]},{"say":"Step 2: Two paths that never meet. Hot water runs inside 61 thin tubes. Cold water runs around the outside of them, inside the shell. They never touch.","do":["set m view=side cut=1 hi=shell labels=tubes,shell"]},{"say":"Step 3: Heat walks through the wall. Each tube wall is just 1 mm of metal. Water can't pass, but heat can: it always flows from hot to cold, right through the metal.","do":["set m view=close cut=1 hi=wall labels=wall"]},{"say":"Step 4: Baffles stir the cold side. These plates make the cold water zigzag back and forth across the tubes, so it brushes past all of them.","do":["set m view=side hi=baffles labels=baffles"]},{"say":"Step 5: The chart tells the story. Hot water falls from 90 to 43 °C. Cold water climbs from 20 to 67 °C. Same 20 L/min on each side, and not one drop crosses over.","do":["set m view=side hi= labels=hotOut,coldOut"]},{"say":"Step 6: Your car has one. A car radiator does the same job. Hot coolant runs inside thin tubes, highway air blows past outside, and 31 kW moves across.","do":["set m view=radiator cut=0 mt=402 hi= labels=radTubes,fins,air"]}]}

name: fighter-3d
desc: 3D working model: afterburner, fast jet, supersonic flight, turbojet vs turbofan, low-bypass turbofan, variable nozzle, shock wave, intake, Mach number, delta wing. views: whole engine core rear intakeMouth. parts: intake (Intake), fan (Fan), bypassDuct (Bypass duct), coreAir (Core air), compressor (Compressor), combustor (Main burner), turbine (Turbines and shafts), afterburner (Afterburner pipe), nozzle (Variable nozzle), jetExhaust (Jet), shockWave (Shock waves), airframe (Delta wing). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 fan revolution; mt windows: 0-10 parked full power, 10-20 parked afterburner (lights at 10), 20-30 parked with the bypass duct shut (same engine as a turbojet), 30-40 flying at 36,000 ft without afterburner (Mach 0.9, Mach 1.0 from t=34), 40-50 flying with afterburner (lights at 40, Mach 1.6 from t=44). shows: air through the intake, 3-stage fan, bypass duct and core; both streams meet behind the turbine; the long afterburner pipe with spray bars and flameholder rings, cold when off, full of flame when lit; the variable nozzle opening wider when the afterburner lights, narrowing then widening again; thrust and fuel with and without the afterburner; pressure in each burner and the oxygen left in the gas; the bypass duct shutting to compare a turbojet with a turbofan of the same thrust; flight at 36,000 ft through Mach 1 to Mach 1.6, thrust against drag, shock waves at the nose, air slowed down before the fan. readouts: thrust and drag (lb), fuel (gal/min), air in (lb/s), Mach number, speed and speed of sound (mph), jet speed (mph), air speed at the fan (mph, Mach), gas temperatures (°F), burner pressures (psi), nozzle throat (in), oxygen left (%), bypass ratio, altitude (ft). not in the model, never say it is shown: landing gear, radar, fuel tank, fuel pump, gearbox, starter, elevon, rudder, flap, thrust vectoring, pylon, ejection seat. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=fighter"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Full power, no extras. Behind the turbines sits a long pipe with spray bars and flame rings. The gas passing through is about 1,200 °F and still has 76% of its oxygen unburned.","do":["set m view=engine cut=1 speed=0.15 hi=afterburner labels=afterburner,turbine"]},{"say":"Step 3: Light it. An afterburner sprays fuel straight into that hot gas and burns the leftover oxygen. The gas jumps to about 3,300 °F, and only 23% of the oxygen is left.","do":["set m view=engine speed=0.2 mt=10 hi=afterburner labels=afterburner"]},{"say":"Step 4: The nozzle opens. Hotter gas takes up more room, so the nozzle opens from 18 to 23 inches across. If it stayed narrow, the gas would back up into the engine.","do":["set m view=rear cut=1 speed=0.15 hi=nozzle labels=nozzle"]},{"say":"Step 5: A big kick. The jet now leaves at 2,600 mph. Thrust climbs from 17,000 to 26,000 lb, about 50% more, just when the airplane needs it.","do":["set m view=whole cut=0 speed=0.15 hi=jetExhaust labels=jetExhaust"]},{"say":"Step 6: Why it is so thirsty. Fuel jumps from 30 to 97 gallons a minute, over 3 times as much. The main burner works at 350 psi but this pipe at only 62 psi. name: forklift-3d
desc: 3D working model: forklift, lift truck, stability triangle, center of gravity, counterweight, tipping, moment, torque, seesaw, lever, mast, lift chain, pulley, movable pulley, mechanical advantage, hydraulic cylinder, rear-wheel steering, turning radius, warehouse. views: side mast head top floor. parts: forks (Forks), mast (Sliding mast), chains (Lift chains and pulley wheel), cylinder (Lift cylinder), load (Crate), counterweight (Iron counterweight), frontAxle (Front wheels (the pivot)), steerAxle (Back wheels (steering)), triangle (Stability triangle), cg (Center of gravity), sweep (Room to turn), wideSweep (With front steering). effects: xray. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: lift 0-30 (rolls in 0-5, picks up crate 5-8, holds at 8 in to 14, lifts to 130 in 14-19.85, holds); Empty, it sits 31 in behind the front wheels.","do":["set m view=side speed=1 mt=0 labels=forks,load,cg"]},{"say":"Step 2: It's a seesaw. The front wheels are the pivot. The crate pushes down 42 in ahead of them: 17,500 lb-ft trying to tip the truck. The 8,500 lb truck, 31 in behind, holds with 21,960 lb-ft. The truck wins.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.6 mt=5 hi=frontAxle labels=frontAxle,load"]},{"say":"Step 3: Heavy on purpose. The crate pulled it forward, 4 in behind the front edge.","do":["set m view=floor xray=0.85 hi=triangle,cg labels=triangle,cg"]},{"say":"Step 5: The limit is a number. Lifted straight up, the balance point stays 4 in behind the front edge but climbs to 76 in. Now a sideways lean of only 12° tips it, down from 30° at floor level. desc: 3D working model: refrigerator, fridge, air conditioner, AC, heat pump, vapor compression, refrigerant, compressor, condenser, evaporator, expansion valve, reversing valve, heat transfer, boiling and pressure, phase change, thermodynamics, COP, home heating. views: fridge fridgeBack house outdoor indoor. parts: compressor (Compressor), condenser (Condenser coils), expansion (Expansion valve), evaporator (Evaporator coils), reversing (Reversing valve), hotGas (Hot gas), warmLiquid (Warm liquid), coldLiquid (Cold liquid), coolGas (Cool gas), cabinet (Food space), outdoor (Outdoor unit), indoor (Indoor unit). effects: cut xray. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: refrigerator 0-40, AC 40-80, reversing valve slides 80-84 (start step 2 of an answer around 78), heat pump 84-124. Speed 1 reads well; the flow is slowed. shows: refrigerator with its side off: food space, freezer, evaporator coils on the freezer back, condenser coils and compressor on the back; house cut open with an indoor unit (coil, blower, duct, ceiling vent) and an outdoor unit (coil, fan, compressor, reversing valve, expansion valve), pipes between them; refrigerant as beads in see-through pipes: close and big when liquid, small and far apart when gas, blue when cold, red when hot; red arrows showing which way heat moves; room and outside air colored by temperature; compressor with its shell see-through: piston moving; reversing valve sliding: hot gas switches from the outdoor coil to the house, flow through both coils runs backward, coils swap jobs; season change: summer with sun and grass, winter with snow. readouts: coil temperatures (°F), pressures (psi above normal air), gas temperature leaving the compressor (°F), room, food space, freezer, kitchen and outside temperatures (°F), air in and out of the indoor unit (°F), heat moved (BTU/h), power (W), BTU/h per watt, times better than a plain heater. not in the model, never say it is shown: thermostat, capillary tube, filter drier, accumulator, defrost heater, defrost cycle, ice maker, water line, door seal, pilot valve, scroll, backup heat, humidity, drain. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=fridge"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: It moves heat out. A refrigerator does not make cold. It carries heat out of the food space and leaves it in the kitchen. The red arrows show the heat. A liquid called refrigerant does the carrying, round and round a sealed loop.","do":["set m view=fridge cut=1 speed=1 mt=0 hi=cabinet labels=cabinet"]},{"say":"Step 2: Liquid boils, soaking up heat. Cold refrigerant enters the evaporator coils at -10 °F, far colder than the 37 °F food space. Heat flows into it and it boils into a gas, like water boiling, only far colder.","do":["set m view=fridge hi=evaporator labels=evaporator,coldLiquid,coolGas"]},{"say":"Step 3: Squeeze the gas. The compressor squeezes the gas from 2 to 135 psi. Squeezing a gas heats it, up to 190 °F. Now it is much hotter than the 72 °F kitchen.","do":["set m view=fridgeBack xray=0.9 hi=compressor labels=compressor,coolGas,hotGas"]},{"say":"Step 4: Give the heat away. Hot gas runs through the condenser coils on the back. At 105 °F they are hotter than the 72 °F kitchen, so heat flows out into the room. Losing heat turns the gas back into a liquid.","do":["set m view=fridgeBack xray=0 hi=condenser labels=condenser,warmLiquid"]},{"say":"Step 5: Drop the pressure. The liquid squeezes through a tiny opening, the expansion valve. Pressure falls from 135 to 2 psi. At low pressure it boils easily and part of it flashes to gas, which chills the rest to -10 °F. The loop starts again.","do":["set m view=fridgeBack hi=expansion labels=expansion,warmLiquid,coldLiquid"]},{"say":"Step 6: Why the back feels warm. It takes in 560 BTU/h from the food, and the motor adds 410 BTU/h. Out the back comes 970 BTU/h. desc: 3D working model: gear types, kinds of gears, spur gear, bevel gear, worm gear, worm and wheel, rack and pinion, planetary gear, sun gear, planet gear, ring gear, gear ratio, gear teeth, speed and torque, self-locking, steering, hand drill, garage door opener, can opener. views: bench spurBevel wormSet wormMesh rackPlanet. parts: spur (Spur gears), bevel (Bevel gears), worm (Worm), wormWheel (Worm wheel), load (Load on a drum), thrust (Tooth pushes along the worm), pinion (Pinion), rack (Rack), sun (Sun gear), planets (Planet gears), ringGear (Ring gear (fixed)), carrier (Carrier (output)). effects: none. clock: 40× slow motion (every input turns once per 2 model s). The worm runs on fixed windows, jump with mt: lifting 0-20, motor off and holding 20-36, driven back down 36-56, holding 56-64 (then repeats); the other sets never stop. shows: five gear sets on one bench, all at 1,200 rpm and 2 N·m in, with teeth that touch and never overlap; spur 18 → 54 (3 : 1): 400 rpm, 5.9 N·m, with twist arrows as thick as the torque; bevel 16 → 32 (2 : 1) turning the drive through 90°: 600 rpm, 3.9 N·m; worm and wheel, one thread → 30 teeth (30 : 1): 40 rpm, up to 26 N·m, 43 % efficient, lifting a 10 kg load on a drum; holding with the motor off: tooth pushes 39 N along the worm, only 3.9 N tries to turn it, friction holds with 4.9 N; arrows as long as the forces; rack and pinion, 20-tooth pinion: 314 mm of rack per turn, 38 N push, moving back and forth; planetary set, sun 18, three planets 18, ring 54 fixed (4 : 1): carrier 300 rpm, 7.8 N·m. readouts: teeth, ratio, input and output speed (rpm), input and output torque (N·m), power (W), rack speed (m/s), rack travel per turn (mm), push on rack (N), efficiency (%), thread angle (°), load (kg), load torque (N·m), worm forces (N). not in the model, never say it is shown: bearing, housing, oil, grease, helical gear, herringbone gear, crown gear, clutch, chain, two-start worm, ball screw, differential. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=geartypes"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Five ways to pass on a turn. Every set on this bench starts at the same 1,200 rpm, shown in slow motion. Teeth lock together so nothing slips, but each set changes the turn in its own way.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.6 mt=0 labels=spur,bevel,worm,rack,ringGear"]},{"say":"Step 2: Spur: side by side. Straight teeth link two parallel shafts. 18 teeth drive 54, a 3 : 1 ratio, so 1,200 rpm becomes 400 rpm. A hand can opener uses a small pair like this.","do":["set m view=spurBevel speed=0.5 hi=spur labels=spur"]},{"say":"Step 3: Bevel: around a corner. Cone-shaped gears send the turn around a 90° corner. 16 teeth drive 32, a 2 : 1 ratio. In a hand drill, the crank turns one way and the bit spins another.","do":["set m view=spurBevel speed=0.5 hi=bevel labels=bevel"]},{"say":"Step 4: Worm: a huge slowdown. One screw thread drives a wheel with 30 teeth, a 30 : 1 ratio in very little space: 1,200 rpm becomes 40 rpm. A garage door opener uses one for its slow, strong pull.","do":["set m view=wormSet speed=1 mt=2 hi=worm,wormWheel labels=worm,wormWheel"]},{"say":"Step 5: Rack and pinion: turn to slide. A round pinion pushes a straight toothed bar. Each turn here moves the rack 314 mm. In a car's steering, the rack pushes the front wheels left and right.","do":["set m view=rackPlanet speed=0.3 hi=pinion,rack labels=pinion,rack"]},{"say":"Step 6: Planetary: small and strong. A sun gear turns three planets inside a fixed ring, and the carrier comes out 4 times slower, 300 rpm, on the same line. A cordless drill packs these behind its chuck.","do":["set m view=rackPlanet speed=0.8 hi=planets labels=sun,planets,ringGear,carrier"]}]}

name: glider-3d
desc: 3D working model: glider, sailplane, soaring, glide ratio, glide angle, lift to drag, L/D, thermal, rising air, aerotow, no engine, lift, drag, weight, sink rate, banking. views: threeq side tow glide chase climb wide. parts: wings (Long wings), body (Body and cockpit), tail (Tail), towPlane (Tow plane), towRope (Tow rope), lift (Lift), weight (Weight), drag (Drag), pull (Forward pull of gravity), glideAngle (Glide angle), thermal (Rising air (thermal)), path (Path flown). effects: none. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second; fixed windows, jump with mt: tow 0-14, release 14-18, glide 18-40, thermal 40-120. shows: tow: small plane pulls the glider on a 200 ft rope at 70 mph, climbing 600 ft/min, rope pull about 110 lb; release at 3,000 ft: rope off, the tow plane peels away left and up, the glider slows from 70 to 64 mph; still-air glide at 64 mph: lift = weight = 880 lb, drag = forward pull of gravity = 22 lb (drag and pull drawn 30x longer); glide ratio 40 : 1 drawn true as 40 marks and a 1 block, glide angle 1.4°, forward 5,600 ft/min, sink 140 ft/min, reach 23 mi and about 21 min from 3,000 ft, small plane 9 : 1 for comparison; thermal: a column of rising air (590 ft/min) over a warm field with a cloud on top; the glider banks 40°, circle radius 320 ft, 22 s a circle, lift 1,150 lb, sinks 190 ft/min, net climb 400 ft/min, about 150 ft per circle, spiral path drawn. readouts: speed (mph), altitude (ft), sink and climb (ft/min), air rising (ft/min), lift, weight, drag, forward pull (lb), glide ratio, glide angle (°), forward speed (ft/min), reach (mi), time left (min), wingspan (ft), span ÷ width, bank (°), circle radius (ft), seconds per circle, gain per circle (ft), rope length (ft) and pull (lb). not in the model, never say it is shown: aileron, rudder, elevator, flap, spoiler, airbrake, wheel, skid, tow hook, winch, instrument panel, variometer, water ballast, parachute, radio, control stick, ridge lift, wave lift. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=glider"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: First, it needs a tow. A glider has no engine, so a small plane pulls it up on a 200 ft rope, at 70 mph.","do":["set m view=tow speed=1 mt=4 hi=towPlane,towRope labels=towPlane,towRope"]},{"say":"Step 2: Then it lets go. At 3,000 ft the pilot lets go of the rope. Nothing pushes the glider now. All it has is its height and speed.","do":["set m view=tow speed=1 mt=12 hi=towRope labels=towRope"]},{"say":"Step 3: Moving air holds it up. At 64 mph, the long wings push air down and the air pushes back up. That lift, 880 lb, matches its 880 lb weight.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0.5 mt=20 hi=wings,lift,weight labels=wings,lift,weight"]},{"say":"Step 4: But drag slows it. Air holds it back with 22 lb of drag. With no engine, what stops it from slowing down? Drag is drawn 30 times longer here.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 hi=drag labels=drag"]},{"say":"Step 5: It flies gently downhill. Like a bike coasting down a long slope, gravity pulls it along its path. That pull, 22 lb, cancels the 22 lb of drag. Both arrows are drawn 30 times longer.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 hi=pull,drag labels=pull,drag"]},{"say":"Step 6: So it sinks, slowly. It always sinks, but only 140 ft/min. From 3,000 ft, still air gives it about 21 minutes in the sky.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0.5 hi= labels=lift,weight"]}]}

name: governor-3d
desc: 3D working model: flywheel, centrifugal governor, flyball governor, speed control, feedback, throttle valve, energy storage, rotational kinetic energy, moment of inertia, E = ½Iω², four-stroke cycle, power stroke, torque ripple, load change, droop. views: bench flywheel engine governor linkage. parts: flywheel (Flywheel), crankshaft (Crankshaft), piston (Piston and rod), cylinder (Cylinder), balls (Flyballs), sleeve (Sliding sleeve), drive (Governor drive), linkage (Lever and rod), throttle (Throttle valve), brake (Water brake), trace (Speed trace). effects: xray. clock: 1 model s = 1 real s (a script's speed slows it). 0-12 flywheel run, 50 N·m, fixed throttle: on until 8, unclutched and sliding off 8-8.3. 20-40 rod unhooked, 40-60 rod hooked: both 30 N·m, 70 N·m from +4 to +14, then 30 N·m. 70-90 energy run: 300 rpm no load full throttle up to 600 by about 73, holds it; at 80 fuel off and 70 N·m; 300 rpm by about 87. In the two slow windows (20-60, 70-90) parts are drawn turning at 1/6 of true rate. Jump with mt. shows: one-cylinder four-stroke engine, 1.8 L, 600 rpm, piston and gas in x-ray, power stroke once per 2 turns; 120 kg spoked iron flywheel, 100 kg in the rim, I = 10.37 kg·m² (a solid disc of the same mass: 7.35); live speed trace with the flywheel (597-611 rpm, swing 14) and without (426-713 rpm, swing 287), power strokes shaded; flywheel unclutches and slides along the shaft at 8 s, coasting; flyball governor: 2 x 3 kg balls on 0.25 m arms, belt and bevel drive 8:1, force arrows (outward pull, weight), sliding sleeve, lever, rod, butterfly throttle valve in a clear body; live speed trace with the rod unhooked (605 falling to 444 rpm) and hooked up (604 to 586 rpm) for a load step 30 to 70 N·m; throttle 30% to 60% as the load rises, ball angle 51° to 48°; live chart of E = ½Iω²: 5,117 J at 300 rpm, 20,468 J at 600 rpm; run-down into the brake with the fuel off. readouts: speed (rpm), swing (rpm), load (N·m), throttle (%), ball angle (°), pull and weight (N), mass (kg), I (kg·m²), ω (rad/s), energy (J), cylinder pressure (kPa), work per cycle (J). not in the model, never say it is shown: spark plug, valve spring, camshaft, carburetor, fuel tank, fuel line, radiator, dashpot, oil pump, generator, steam, starter, muffler, turbine. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=governor"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A heavy wheel on the shaft. This engine runs at about 600 rpm against a water brake. On its shaft sits a 120 kg iron flywheel.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.12 mt=2 labels=flywheel,brake"]},{"say":"Step 2: Only one stroke pushes. The piston pushes only on the power stroke, one stroke in four. In the other three, the shaft must keep turning with no push at all.","do":["set m view=engine xray=0.9 speed=0.08 hi=piston labels=piston,crankshaft"]},{"say":"Step 3: It soaks up and pays back. Each power stroke gives the wheel extra energy. It pays it back between pushes. Speed only swings 14 rpm, from 597 to 611.","do":["set m view=bench xray=0 speed=0.15 hi=trace"]},{"say":"Step 4: Take the flywheel away. Now we unclutch it and slide it along the shaft. It coasts by itself. Same engine, same load, same throttle.","do":["set m view=flywheel speed=0.15 mt=7.7 hi=flywheel labels=flywheel"]},{"say":"Step 5: Now the speed lurches. With nothing to store energy, the shaft speeds up on each push and sags after it. It swings 287 rpm, from 426 to 713.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.15 mt=9 hi=trace"]},{"say":"Step 6: So what does it do?. A flywheel stores energy to smooth the speed inside each cycle. It does not make power, and it cannot set the speed.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.15 hi=flywheel,trace labels=flywheel"]}]}

name: gyroscope-3d
desc: 3D working model: gyroscope, angular momentum, torque, precession, spin, moment of inertia, right-hand rule, why a bike stays up, bicycle balance, bicycle wheel, steering geometry, trail, gyroscopic effect, rolling wheel, self-stability. views: stand close above wheelRoad bike. parts: wheel (Wheel), axle (Axle), pivot (Free pivot), stand (Stand), angularMomentum (Angular momentum, L), torque (Torque), weight (Weight of the wheel), path (Path it circles), bikeWheel (Bicycle wheel), steering (Steering (fork and bars)), bikeBody (Bicycle and test rider), track (Tire track). effects: none. clock: model time is real seconds, wheel drawn turning 25x slower than its readout. 0-60 = wheel at 3000 rpm let go at t 0; 100-130 = same wheel no spin let go at t 100, hangs in 0.2 s (use speed about 0.06); 140-200 = 1500 rpm let go at t 140; 210-240 = on its rest, spun up 0 to 3000 rpm over t 210-220; 300-340 = bicycle wheel alone rolling at 5 m/s leaning 5°; 400-420 = bicycle held at a 5° lean (use speed 0); these bicycle runs all get the same sideways nudge 1 s in: 420-440 hands off, 5 m/s; 440-460 steering locked; 460-480 wheels' spin removed, hands off; 480-500 hands off at 1.5 m/s; 500-520 spin removed, rider steering. Jump with mt. shows: a 0.50 kg, 7.5 cm wheel on an axle 0.12 m from a free pivot, let go level at 3000 rpm: it dips only about 1.4° and circles at 1.33 rad/s, once every 4.7 s; the same wheel with no spin: it falls, hanging straight down in 0.2 s, then swings and settles; half the spin (1500 rpm), half the angular momentum (0.22 kg·m²/s), twice the circling rate (2.66 rad/s); angular momentum arrow along the axle, growing as the wheel spins up; torque arrow from gravity (4.9 N at 0.12 m is 0.59 N·m), sideways at the arrow's tip; a bicycle wheel alone (3.0 kg, 0.28 kg·m²) at 5 m/s, 136 rpm: L 4.0 kg·m²/s, leaning 5° it curves into the lean at 0.10 rad/s; a bicycle and rigid test rider (94 kg) at a 5° lean: 69 N·m of tipping torque against 6.0 kg·m²/s from both wheels; the same bicycle nudged at 5 m/s hands off: steers itself up to 4.6°, leans at most 4.2°, recovers; tire track shows the wheels moving under the lean; steering locked: down in under 1 s, wheels still spinning; the wheels' spin removed, hands off: it also falls, because the front wheel's spin is part of what starts the steering; the wheels' spin removed, rider steering: stays up, biggest lean 1.8°; hands off at 1.5 m/s: falls; the stable hands-off range of this bicycle is 4.3 to 6.0 m/s. readouts: spin (rpm, rad/s), mass (kg), weight (N), arm (m), torque (N·m), angular momentum (kg·m²/s), spin inertia (kg·m²), precession (rad/s), angle below level (°), speed (m/s), lean and steer (°), head angle (°), trail (m). not in the model, never say it is shown: motor, pull cord, gimbal, gyrocompass, drone, spacecraft, pedal, chain, gear, brake, kickstand, training wheel, helmet. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=gyroscope"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Not spinning: it falls. This wheel hangs out from a free pivot, with nothing under it. Let go with no spin and it drops, hanging straight down in just 0.2 s. Shown here in slow motion.","do":["set m view=stand speed=0.06 mt=100 labels=wheel,pivot"]},{"say":"Step 2: Spinning: it stays up. Same wheel, same pivot, now spinning at 3,000 rpm. Let go and it stays almost level, dipping only a little. Instead of falling, it starts moving sideways.","do":["set m view=stand speed=0.5 mt=0 hi=wheel labels=wheel"]},{"say":"Step 3: Gravity still pulls. Slowed way down now. The wheel weighs 4.9 N and sits 0.12 m from the pivot. That makes a torque, a twist, of 0.59 N·m. Torque is the red arrow.","do":["set m view=close speed=0.05 mt=4.4 hi=weight,torque labels=weight,torque"]},{"say":"Step 4: Spin has a direction. Spin carries angular momentum, L, the blue arrow, 0.44 kg·m²/s along the axle. A torque changes L in the torque's own direction. That is sideways, so the arrow swings sideways.","do":["set m view=close speed=0.05 hi=angularMomentum,torque labels=angularMomentum,torque"]},{"say":"Step 5: So it circles. The wheel follows its turning arrow around the stand at 1.33 rad/s, once every 4.7 s. This circling is called precession. The torque keeps turning L, and never gets to tip the wheel.","do":["set m view=above speed=1 mt=8 hi=path,angularMomentum,torque labels=path"]},{"say":"Step 6: Less spin, faster circle. At half the spin, 1,500 rpm, L is only 0.22 kg·m²/s. The same torque turns the smaller arrow twice as fast, 2.66 rad/s. Real wheels slow down, so in the end they do tip.","do":["set m view=above speed=1 mt=150 hi=path,angularMomentum,torque labels=path"]}]}

name: helicopter-3d
desc: 3D working model: helicopter, rotor, hover, lift, collective, cyclic, swashplate, tail rotor, torque, Newton's third law, forward flight, downwash, pedals. views: side threeq hub top tail. parts: blades (Main rotor blades), mast (Mast and hub), swashplate (Swashplate), pitchLinks (Pitch links), gearbox (Engine and gearbox), tailRotor (Tail rotor), fuselage (Cabin and tail boom), downwash (Air pushed down), pedals (Pedals), lift (Lift), weight (Weight), torque (Twist on the body), tailPush (Tail rotor push). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second (slow it with speed); fixed windows, jump with mt: lift-off and hover 0-12, climb 12-24, forward flight 24-64, tail rotor 64-80. shows: collective: the swashplate slides up and both blades pitch up together (0° on the ground, 7.7° hover, 9.1° lift-off peak, 8.6° climbing steadily at 13 ft/s); lift and weight arrows; lift as % of weight (120 % at lift-off, 100 % in hover); air pushed down through the rotor (33 mph below it in hover) and spreading along the ground; cyclic: the swashplate tilts, pitch changes around the circle, the rotor disk tips forward (up to 17.8° speeding up, 7.6° at 101 mph); the body tipping nose-down with the rotor in forward flight (10.6° speeding up, 4.5° cruising); air streaming past in forward flight, bent down behind the rotor; torque reaction: the twist on the body (910 lb-ft) and the tail rotor push that cancels it (60 lb at 15 ft); the body spinning the other way when the tail push drops out, and stopping again; the pilot's pedals moving with the tail rotor push (x-ray). readouts: collective pitch, lift as % of weight, height, climb rate, downwash speed, engine power (hp), airspeed (mph), rotor tilt, nose-down tilt, forward pull (lb), rotor torque (lb-ft), tail rotor push (lb), body spin (°/s), rotor rpm. not in the model, never say it is shown: cyclic stick, collective lever, drive belt, tail rotor drive shaft, flybar, scissor link, ground effect, instrument panel, seat, door, fuel tank, clutch, autorotation. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=helicopter"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Wings that spin. The long blades on top are wings that spin around 530 times a minute. Right now they are flat, at 0°, so they slice the air and make no lift.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0.25 mt=0 labels=blades,mast"]},{"say":"Step 2: Tilt every blade. The pilot raises a lever. The swashplate slides up the mast and the pitch links twist both blades the same amount: 4.1° and rising. Tilted blades push air down.","do":["set m view=hub speed=0.22 mt=1.5 hi=swashplate,pitchLinks labels=swashplate,pitchLinks,blades"]},{"say":"Step 3: Lift beats weight. A little more pitch and the lift passes the weight, so the helicopter rises. At 5 ft up the pilot is already easing back: 8.0°, lift 97 % of the weight, so the rise slows.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.45 mt=3 hi=lift labels=lift,weight"]},{"say":"Step 4: Hover: lift = weight. At 7.7° the lift is exactly 100 % of the weight. The rotor throws air down at about 33 mph, and the air pushes the rotor up just as hard.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.12 mt=7 hi=downwash labels=downwash,lift,weight"]},{"say":"Step 5: More pitch to climb. To go up, the pilot adds pitch, to 9.1°. The helicopter climbs at 13 ft/s, and the engine works harder: 117 hp instead of 92 hp in the hover.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 mt=13 hi=blades labels=blades,lift"]}]}

name: hybrid-3d
desc: 3D working model: hybrid car, power-split, planetary gear, motor-generator, regenerative braking, regen, city vs highway mpg, gas mileage, plug-in hybrid vs hybrid vs electric, energy flow, engine off at stops, battery size, kWh. views: hero flow drive gears rear. parts: body (Car body), engine (Gas engine), tank (Gas tank), mg1 (Small motor-generator), mg2 (Big motor-generator), sun (Sun gear), carrier (Carrier and pinions), ring (Ring gear), battery (Battery), inverter (Inverter), gears (Gears to the wheels), wheels (Drive wheels). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second of the drive; spinning parts are drawn at 1/20 real speed. Fixed windows, jump with mt: low 0-20 (stopped 1 s, pulls away on battery, holds 20 mph), charge 20-35 (25 mph, engine charging a low battery), cruise 35-55 (65 mph), hard 55-80 (stopped 1 s, flat out to 70 mph), brake 80-100 (normal stop from 40 mph), city 100-170 (stop and go, 12 s stopped, up to 35 mph, 15 s hold, stop). Cut works only from a view on the +z side (gears view). Arrows show only with x-ray on and no cut.. shows: energy arrows in every mode: red gas power, blue electric, green back from braking; size follows the power; low speed: engine off, battery to big motor to wheels, small motor spinning backward with no load; cruise at 65 mph: engine 2,290 rpm, 18 hp, about 90% straight through the gears, 10% through the small motor; the planetary set face on (sun 30, 4 pinions of 24, ring 78): 72% of engine twist to ring, 28% to sun; the three speeds tied by one law; hard acceleration: engine 98 hp plus battery, up to about 115 hp at the wheels; 0-60 mph in about 9 s; braking: big motor generates, 0.047 kWh back from a 40 mph stop, engine off; charging on the move with the engine: small motor feeds the battery; no plug needed; four pistons, crank, and rods moving inside the faded engine, stopped when the engine is off; trip results from the same math: 56 mpg city, 49 highway, engine on 15% of the city trip; a gas-only car of this size 24 and 43 (numbers only); comparison numbers only (not on screen as objects): plug-in hybrid about 13 kWh, 40 miles; electric car about 75 kWh, 300 miles. readouts: speed (mph), engine (rpm, hp), battery power in or out (hp), power at the wheels (hp), motor powers (hp), sun, carrier and ring speeds (rpm), teeth, twist split (%), road power (hp), air and tire share (%), battery size and energy back (kWh), battery charge (%), battery-alone range (miles), city and highway (mpg). not in the model, never say it is shown: radiator, coolant, exhaust, muffler, starter, alternator, differential, spark plug, fuel pump, fuel injector, 12-volt battery, pedal, steering, suspension, dashboard, second reduction gear, CV joint. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=hybrid"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Gas and electric, in one car. A hybrid has a gas engine and two electric motors. A computer picks the best mix every moment. You just drive.","do":["set m view=hero speed=1 mt=43 labels=body"]},{"say":"Step 2: Slow: battery only. At 20 mph the car needs very little. The engine stays off. The battery sends just 3 hp of electricity to the big motor, and that turns the wheels.","do":["set m view=flow xray=0.95 speed=1 mt=9 hi=mg2 labels=battery,mg2"]},{"say":"Step 3: Cruising: gas does the work. At 65 mph the engine runs at 2,290 rpm and makes 18 hp. Most of that goes straight through gears to the wheels. The battery rests.","do":["set m view=drive xray=0.95 speed=1 mt=42 hi= labels=engine,gears,wheels"]},{"say":"Step 4: One set of gears joins it all. Engine on the carrier, small motor on the sun, big motor and wheels on the ring. Every turn of the engine splits: 72% of its twist to the ring, 28% to the sun.","do":["set m view=gears cut=1 speed=0.3 mt=44 hi=sun,carrier,ring labels=sun,carrier,ring"]},{"say":"Step 5: Hard acceleration: everything. Floor it. The engine jumps to 5,200 rpm and 98 hp, the small motor makes electricity, the battery adds 30 hp, and the big motor pushes hard.","do":["set m view=drive cut=0 speed=1 mt=59.5 hi=mg2 labels=mg1,mg2"]},{"say":"Step 6: Braking: energy comes back. The wheels now spin the big motor, so it makes electricity. At 24 mph, 19 hp flows into the battery instead of turning into brake heat.","do":["set m view=flow speed=1 mt=83 hi=battery labels=battery,wheels"]}]}

name: hydraulic-3d
desc: 3D working model: hydraulics, pressure, Pascal's principle, hydraulic jack, hydraulic press, car brakes, brake fluid, force multiplier, area, work, lever, one-way valve, brake booster. views: jack valves car brakes caliper. parts: lever (Handle), smallPiston (Small piston), bigPiston (Big piston), valve (One-way valve), reservoir (Oil tank), oil (Oil), car (Car), pedal (Brake pedal), booster (Brake booster), master (Master cylinder), brakeLine (Brake line), caliper (Caliper piston), disc (Brake disc). effects: xray. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: jack 0-204 (one pump every 2 s, pump k starts at 2k, push 0.2-1.1 s into it, lift 1.3-1.9 s; name: hydro-3d

name: instruments-3d
desc: 3D working model: airspeed, pitot tube, static port, altimeter, air pressure, altitude, attitude indicator, gyroscope, flight instruments, flying in clouds, dynamic pressure. views: bench pitot airspeed altimeter attitude. parts: pitot (Pitot tube), staticPort (Static port), pitotLine (Pitot line), staticLine (Static line), airspeed (Airspeed indicator), diaphragm (Diaphragm), altimeter (Altimeter), aneroid (Sealed capsules), gears (Gears), attitude (Attitude indicator), gyro (Spinning gyro), horizon (Horizon). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second of flight, except the gyro wheel, drawn slowed down. 0-30 speeding up to 120 knots at sea level; 30-64 climbing to 8,000 ft; 66-105 in a cloud, banking 30° right then 30° left (only the attitude indicator and its panel show there). shows: air ramming into the pitot tube while it only slides past the static port; airspeed indicator cut open: pitot air inside a diaphragm, static air around it, the stretch driving a toothed sector, a pinion and the needle; twice the speed makes four times the pressure difference, on a dial with crowded low speeds; altimeter cut open: sealed capsules growing as the outside air thins, gears, a long hand (1,000 ft a turn) and a short hand (10,000 ft a turn); attitude indicator cut open: a spinning gyro wheel and the horizon stay level while the case and panel bank around them. readouts: airspeed (knots), altitude (ft), static and pitot pressure (inHg), pressure difference (inHg), hand turns, bank angle (°), gyro speed (rpm). not in the model, never say it is shown: vacuum pump, electric motor, erecting mechanism, drain hole, heater, vertical speed indicator, turn coordinator, compass, pitch, autopilot, air data computer, alternate static source, hairspring, third hand. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=instruments"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: No road to measure. The pitot tube has an open mouth facing forward. At 60 knots, air gets jammed in. Pressure inside rises to 30.09 inHg.","do":["set m view=pitot cut=1 hi=pitot labels=pitot"]},{"say":"Step 3: Air slides past the hole. The static port is a little hole facing sideways. Air slides past it without ramming in, so it feels only the plain outside pressure, 29.92 inHg.","do":["set m view=pitot hi=staticPort labels=staticPort"]},{"say":"Step 4: A pressure tug-of-war. name: ion-3d

An electron source fires 13 A of electrons (gold dots). Magnet rings keep them bouncing, so they smash into xenon atoms and knock electrons off. Each hit atom becomes a charged ion.","do":["set m view=grids xray=0 speed=0.5 hi=electrons,chamber labels=electrons,chamber"]},{"say":"Step 3: Two grids throw the ions. name: lander-3d

desc: 3D working model: loom, weaving, warp, weft, shed, harness, shaft, heddle, reed, beater, shuttle, plain weave, twill, 3/1 twill, denim, jeans, cloth, fabric, indigo, thread. views: whole side shed cloth under. parts: warpBeam (Warp beam), backBeam (Back beam), warp (Warp (blue)), heddles (Heddles), harnesses (Harnesses), levers (Levers), reed (Reed), shuttle (Shuttle), weft (Weft (white)), cloth (Cloth), breastBeam (Front beam), clothBeam (Cloth beam). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 pick (one pass of the shuttle). Model time below 1000 weaves plain weave (harnesses 1+3, 2+4); from 1000 on it weaves 3/1 twill (123, 234, 341, 412), so switch pattern with mt (mt 1000 = first twill pick). The cloth on the loom always shows the pattern being woven. xray fades the frame and beater so harnesses show from the side (use with the side view). The under view looks at the bottom of the cloth.. shows: 96 blue warp ends from the warp beam over the back beam, through heddles on 4 harnesses and an 8-dent reed, to the cloth; levers on the castle lifting harnesses; the warp splitting into a shed 3.5 in open at the heddles; a boat shuttle crossing the shed and laying a white weft, alternating direction each pick; the reed swinging forward to beat the weft into the cloth edge, 8 picks per inch; plain weave (checkerboard, 50% blue each side) and 3/1 twill (diagonal, 75% blue on top, 25% underneath) in the cloth; cloth going over the front beam onto the cloth beam, top and bottom faces. readouts: pattern, pick number, harnesses up, warp ends, ends per inch, width (in), reed dents per inch, picks per inch, picks per minute, shed opening (in), blue on top (%), blue underneath (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: treadle, lamm, ratchet, pawl, lease stick, raddle, temple, fly shuttle, bobbin winder, warping board, jacquard, dobby, power loom, selvage, selvedge, rigid heddle, dye, dyeing, spinning, inkle. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=loom"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Two sets of threads. The shuttle slides through the shed, under the raised threads and over the rest. It unwinds a white weft thread behind it. A weaver does this about 30 times a minute.","do":["set m view=shed xray=0 speed=0.1 mt=2.15 hi=shuttle,weft labels=shuttle,weft"]},{"say":"Step 4: Beat. name: printer-3d
desc: 3D working model: 3D printer, 3D printing, filament, extruder, hot end, nozzle, layers, layer height, overhang, supports, lead screw, belt drive, heated bed. views: wide head axes layers bead. parts: spool (Filament spool), extruderGear (Extruder gear), hotEnd (Hot end), nozzle (Nozzle), xAxis (X axis belt), yAxis (Y axis belt), zScrew (Z lead screw), bed (Heated bed), part (Printed part), slope (Gentle slope), shelf (Flat shelf (overhang)), supports (Supports). effects: xray. clock: Model seconds: 12-52 are real time on the cup (1 model s = 1 real s); other windows are sped up, jobs chosen with mt: cup 0-100, three domes 100-200, overhang piece 200+. shows: filament off a spool, gripped by a toothed gear, pushed into the hot end; plastic melting in the hot end and leaving a 0.4 mm nozzle (x-ray); head moved in X by a belt, bed moved in Y by a belt, gantry lifted in Z by a lead screw; a cup growing layer by layer at life size, 254 layers of 0.2 mm; the same dome at 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 mm: stairs, number of layers, print time; a 45° slope printing fine, a flat shelf drooping into strings, supports under the shelf and snapped off. readouts: hot end and bed temperature (°F), layer height, nozzle, filament, line (mm), part and bed size (in), head speed (in/s), motor rpm, screw turn per layer, layers, print time (min), filament used (ft), share of line over air (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: infill, fan, control board, power supply, display, limit switch, wiring, slicer, resin, laser, enclosure, level sensor, brim, raft. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=printer"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: It draws in melted plastic. The printer draws one thin slice of an object in melted plastic, then the next slice on top. Stack 254 slices and this 2.0 in cup is done.","do":["set m view=wide speed=1.2 mt=2 hi=part labels=spool,part,bed"]},{"say":"Step 2: A gear feeds the plastic. Plastic comes off the spool as a thread called filament, 1.75 mm thick. A toothed gear grips it and pushes it down into the hot end.","do":["set m view=head xray=1 speed=1 mt=14 hi=spool,extruderGear labels=extruderGear"]},{"say":"Step 3: Heat, then squeeze. The hot end melts the plastic at 410 °F. It squeezes out of a 0.4 mm hole as a thin line that comes out 27 times faster than the filament goes in.","do":["set m view=head xray=1 speed=1 hi=hotEnd,nozzle labels=hotEnd,nozzle"]},{"say":"Step 4: Two belts steer it. One belt slides the head left and right. Another slides the bed front and back. Together they trace any shape at 2 in/s.","do":["set m view=axes xray=0 speed=1 hi=xAxis,yAxis labels=xAxis,yAxis"]},{"say":"Step 5: A screw lifts it. When a slice is finished, the lead screw turns 1/10 of a turn. That lifts the head just 0.2 mm, ready for the next slice.","do":["set m view=axes speed=1 hi=zScrew labels=zScrew"]},{"say":"Step 6: The hot bed holds on. The bed stays at 140 °F so the first layer sticks and the part does not curl up. This cup takes about 26 min and 9 ft of filament.","do":["set m view=wide speed=2.8 mt=53 hi=bed labels=bed,part"]}]}

name: pulley-3d
desc: 3D working model: pulley, pulleys, block and tackle, mechanical advantage, simple machines, effort and load, work, crane, tower crane, counterweight, moment, turning effect, levers and balance. views: bench tackle crane counter hook. parts: fixed (Fixed pulley (1 rope)), movable (Movable pulley (2 ropes)), tackle (Block and tackle (4 ropes)), load (Load), hand (Hand pull (effort)), tower (Tower), jib (Jib), counterJib (Counter-jib), counterweight (Counterweight), trolley (Trolley), hookBlock (Hook block (2 rope falls)), winch (Winch drum). effects: none. clock: model seconds 0-10 = pulley bench (loads rise 1.64 ft at t 1-7); jump with mt. shows: the same 220 lb box lifted by a fixed pulley, a movable pulley and a 4-rope block and tackle, side by side; effort = load ÷ number of supporting ropes: 220 / 110 / 55 lb, with effort arrows to scale; rope pulled = ropes × load raised: 1.64 / 3.28 / 6.56 ft for a 1.64 ft lift; sheaves turn with the rope; work in = work out: 55 lb × 6.56 ft = 220 lb × 1.64 ft; tower crane: 2-fall hook block, winch drum winding in 39.4 ft to lift 19.7 ft, winch effort 1,100 lb; moments: load 2,200 lb × trolley distance vs counterweight 8,800 lb × 24.6 ft; balance at 98.4 ft (about 217,000 lb-ft each); without the counterweight: counter moment 0, 217,000 lb-ft unbalanced toward the load, the crane leans toward the load (a gentle capped lean), then stands again when the counterweight goes back; trolley travel does not raise or lower the hook (rope runs to a dead end at the jib tip). readouts: load (lb), effort (lb), mechanical advantage, rope pulled (ft), load raised (ft), trolley out (ft), load moment, counter moment, difference / unbalanced (lb-ft), tips toward. not in the model, never say it is shown: friction, cab, operator, slewing ring, ballast, climbing frame, ladder, brake, limit switch, wind gauge, gear, compound pulley, load chart. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=pulley"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Three ways to lift one box. Each box weighs 220 lb. Gravity pulls it down that hard, so lifting it straight up takes a 220 lb pull.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0 mt=0 labels=fixed,movable,tackle,load"]},{"say":"Step 2: 1 rope: a fixed pulley. One rope holds the box. The pulley only turns your pull around: you pull down to lift up, but you still pull 220 lb.","do":["set m speed=1 mt=1 hi=fixed labels=fixed,hand"]},{"say":"Step 3: 2 ropes: a movable pulley. The pulley rides on the box, so 2 ropes hold it up. Each rope carries half, and your pull drops to 110 lb.","do":["set m speed=1 mt=1 hi=movable labels=movable,hand"]},{"say":"Step 4: 4 ropes: a block and tackle. Two pulleys on top, two on the box. Now 4 ropes share the load, so you pull only 55 lb, a quarter.","do":["set m view=tackle speed=1 mt=1 hi=tackle labels=tackle,hand"]},{"say":"Step 5: Count the ropes. Pull = load ÷ ropes holding it: 220, 110, 55 lb. That number of ropes is the mechanical advantage: 1, 2 or 4.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0 mt=7 hi= labels=fixed,movable,tackle"]}]}

name: ramjet-3d
desc: 3D working model: ramjet, scramjet, air-breathing engine, shock wave, shock cone, diffuser, flame holder, hypersonic flight, supersonic combustion, no moving parts, Mach number. views: hero both ram inlet scram. parts: shockCone (Shock cone), shockWaves (Shock waves), diffuser (Diffuser), fuelBars (Fuel spray bars), flameHolders (Flame holders), nozzle (Nozzle), vehicle (Test vehicle), ramAir (Air through the ramjet), scramInlet (Scramjet inlet), scramBurner (Scramjet burner), scramNozzle (Scramjet nozzle), scramAir (Air through the scramjet). effects: cut. clock: 1 model second = 1 thousandth of a real second, on the same clock for both engines. mt 0 up: cruise (ramjet Mach 3 at 20 km, scramjet Mach 7 at 28 km). mt 1000 up: the ramjet speeding up at one height, on plateaus: Mach 0 at 1000-1008, Mach 1 at 1010-1018, Mach 2 at 1020-1028, Mach 3 from 1030.. shows: a ramjet and a scramjet on plain test vehicles, same intake size, cut open side by side; shock waves off the nose cone reaching the intake lip, and the normal shock in the ramjet's throat; air slowing from Mach 3 to about Mach 0.2 in the ramjet's widening diffuser, getting hotter and squeezed about 30 times; fuel spray bars and flame holders keeping a steady flame in slow air; hot gas squeezing through the nozzle throat and leaving faster than it came in; the ramjet at Mach 0, 1, 2, 3: air frozen at Mach 0, squeeze, air flow and thrust rising with speed; the scramjet keeping air at Mach 2.5 through its burner, with a thin flame and only about 1 thousandth of a second to burn; why Mach 7 air cannot be slowed to subsonic: it would reach about 1,900 °C before any fuel burns. readouts: Mach number (flight and in the burner), pressure (kPa), temperature (°C), thrust (kN), squeeze ratio, air flow (kg/s), air and jet speed (m/s), time in the burner (ms), height (km). not in the model, never say it is shown: booster, rocket, fuel tank, fuel pump, igniter, fuel line, landing gear, cockpit, heat shield, cooling channel, control fin. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=ramjet"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Speed does the squeezing. A ramjet has no fan, no compressor and no turbine. It is a shaped tube. Flying at Mach 3, it uses its own speed to push air in.","do":["set m view=hero speed=1 mt=0 labels=shockCone,nozzle,vehicle"]},{"say":"Step 2: Shock waves. The pointed cone makes shock waves that reach the intake lip. Crossing them, the air suddenly slows down and packs tighter. Nothing has to spin.","do":["set m view=inlet cut=1 speed=1 hi=shockCone,shockWaves labels=shockCone,shockWaves"]},{"say":"Step 3: Slow air, high pressure. The duct gets wider, so the air slows to about Mach 0.2. Its speed turns into pressure: 160 kPa, 30 times the air outside, and about 330 °C.","do":["set m view=ram speed=1 hi=diffuser labels=diffuser,ramAir"]},{"say":"Step 4: Burn. Bars spray in fuel. Flame holders make calm pockets behind them so the flame stays lit and does not blow away. The gas reaches about 1,700 °C.","do":["set m view=ram speed=1 hi=fuelBars,flameHolders labels=fuelBars,flameHolders"]},{"say":"Step 5: Blow. Hot, high-pressure gas rushes through the narrow neck and out at about 1,600 m/s. Air came in at about 890 m/s. That difference is 21 kN of thrust.","do":["set m view=ram speed=1 hi=nozzle labels=nozzle,ramAir"]}]}

name: smallengine-3d
desc: 3D working model: lawn mower engine, small engine, pull start, recoil starter, flywheel, magneto, 2-stroke engine, 4-stroke engine, two-stroke vs four-stroke, chainsaw engine, crankcase ports, transfer port, fuel-oil mix, 2-stroke oil, splash lubrication. views: both mower starter saw sawBack. parts: rope (Pull rope), pawls (Pawls (hooks)), flywheel (Flywheel), coil (Magnet + coil), piston (Mower piston), valves (Valves), sparkPlug (Spark plug), oilPool (Oil pool), sawPiston (Saw piston), transferPort (Transfer port), exhaustPort (Exhaust port), fuelMix (Fuel-oil mix). effects: cut xray. clock: 0-1 s at rest; 1-7 s the rope pull (3 turns, real time 0.6 s), first firing at 5.28 s; after that 1 model second = half a crank turn in slow motion for both engines. This mower engine only runs once it is already turning. So the first turns come from you, through a rope wound on a pulley.","do":["set m view=starter speed=0.15 mt=0 labels=rope,flywheel"]},{"say":"Step 2: Pull: the hooks grab. When you pull, the pulley spins and two small hooks called pawls swing in. They catch the teeth on the flywheel's hub, so now your pull turns the engine.","do":["set m xray=0.9 speed=0.3 mt=1 hi=pawls labels=pawls,rope"]},{"say":"Step 3: A heavy wheel gets moving. name: solidrocket-3d

name: spinning-3d
desc: 3D working model: spinning, ring spinning, spinning frame, spinning machine, cotton, thread, yarn, roving, drafting, draft, rollers, twist, twist per inch, fibers, friction, spindle, bobbin, ring, traveler, thread guide, textile, fabric, cloth. views: whole drafting nip balloon ring. parts: roving (Roving), backRoller (Back rollers), middleRoller (Middle rollers), frontRoller (Front rollers), fibers (Fibers), yarn (Yarn), guide (Thread guide), ring (Ring), traveler (Traveler), spindle (Spindle), bobbin (Bobbin). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 turn of the front roller (0.27 real seconds). In that second the back roller turns 1/30, the middle 1/24, the spindle and traveler about 68 times, and 3.14 in of yarn is made. Use speed 0.3-0.6 to watch the rollers and the strand stretch (marks on the strand spread apart 30x); use speed 0.01-0.03 to watch the spindle, the balloon and the traveler, and the fibers flowing along their spiral in the nip view. The nip view is a close-up just under the front rollers: always use xray 1 with it (fades the top rollers and arm). Fibers there and the yarn everywhere are drawn thicker than real, with the real 24° twist angle. shows: one spinning position: roving bobbin, three pairs of drafting rollers (fluted steel bottom, rubber top), thread guide, ring, traveler, spindle with its tape, bobbin with yarn wound on; the strand stretched 30 times: marks on it spread apart and it thins from round roving to a flat ribbon; rollers turning at their real ratio: back 7.3, middle 9.2, front 220 rpm; a close view of the twist triangle: 32 fibers in a flat ribbon at the nip closing into a twisted yarn; the spiral of twist on the yarn, the whirling yarn loop (balloon) and the traveler running round the ring; numbers for strength: one fiber 0.01 lb, the yarn 0.7 lb; fibers across 3,600 in the roving and 120 in the yarn. readouts: spindle (rpm), front, middle, back roller (rpm), draft, twist (per in), twist angle (degrees), yarn made (ft/min), yarn so far (in), fibers across, fiber length (in), turns per fiber, yarn width (in), fiber and yarn strength (lb), traveler (rpm, mph), spindle lead over traveler (rpm), ring size (in). not in the model, never say it is shown: cotton gin, carding machine, comber, drawing frame, roving frame, apron, suction tube, separator, balloon control ring, builder motion, doffing, motor, tin roller, creel. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=spinning"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: From fluffy boll to soft rope. Picked cotton is cleaned and combed in other machines into a soft rope called roving. It is about 3,600 fibers thick. This frame turns it into thread.","do":["set m view=whole speed=0.02 mt=0 hi=roving labels=roving,bobbin"]},{"say":"Step 2: Stretched thin. Three pairs of rollers grip the roving. Each pair turns faster than the one before. The front rollers turn 220 rpm, 30 times faster than the back ones, so it comes out 30 times thinner.","do":["set m view=drafting speed=0.5 hi=backRoller,middleRoller,frontRoller labels=backRoller,middleRoller,frontRoller"]},{"say":"Step 3: Twisted together. Right under the front rollers, the loose fibers swirl into a tight spiral, 21.7 twists in every inch. Twisted, they grip each other.","do":["set m view=nip xray=1 speed=0.02 hi=fibers labels=fibers,frontRoller"]},{"say":"Step 4: Down to the spindle. The new yarn runs through a thread guide and whirls in a wide loop around the bobbin. The stripes show the spiral of twist.","do":["set m view=balloon xray=0 speed=0.02 hi=guide,yarn labels=guide,yarn"]},{"say":"Step 5: The traveler puts in twist. The spindle spins 15,000 rpm. The yarn drags a tiny clip, the traveler, around the ring at 73 mph. Each lap adds one twist.","do":["set m view=ring speed=0.02 hi=traveler labels=traveler,ring"]},{"say":"Step 6: Wound on the bobbin. The spindle runs 230 rpm ahead of the traveler. name: steam-3d
desc: 3D working model: steam engine, heat engine, locomotive, steam locomotive, boiler, piston, slide valve, double-acting, crank, eccentric, industrial revolution. views: side threeq boiler cylinder motion. parts: firebox (Firebox), boiler (Boiler and fire tubes), steamPipe (Steam pipe), slideValve (Slide valve), cylinder (Cylinder and steam chest), piston (Piston and piston rod), crosshead (Crosshead), conRod (Connecting rod), wheel (Driving wheel and crank), eccentric (Eccentric), chimney (Smokestack), steam (Steam), reverser (Reverse lever). effects: cut xray. clock: model seconds are real seconds: 0-8 s the wheel turns at 15 rpm (one stroke = 2 s), 8-9 s it speeds up, from 9 s it runs at 37 mph (212 rpm; name: stirling-3d
desc: 3D working model: Stirling engine, heat engine, external combustion, regenerator, displacer, pressure-volume diagram, PV loop, temperature difference, thermodynamic cycle, Carnot efficiency. views: threeq section chamber crank plates. parts: heater (Outside heat source), hotPlate (Hot plate), coldPlate (Cold plate with fins), displacer (Displacer), regenerator (Regenerator), powerCylinder (Power cylinder), powerPiston (Power piston), crankshaft (Cranks, 90° apart), flywheel (Flywheel), air (Sealed air). effects: cut. clock: 0-100: steady running, 1 model second = 1 wheel turn. 100-200: cold start, 200-300: more heat, both 1 model second = 30 s on the clock. shows: the four-part cycle: hot air expands, displacer moves it through the regenerator, cold air is squeezed, displacer moves it back; sealed air colored by temperature, hot to cold, flowing through the regenerator and into the power cylinder; a live pressure-volume loop with a moving dot and the work per turn; no difference between the plates means no motion; the wheel starts once the difference reaches 30 °C; slow warm-up and slow response to more heat, with a clock; heat in, power and heat out; best possible efficiency vs this engine. readouts: plate temperatures (°C), pressure (kPa), air volume (cm³), wheel speed (rpm), power (W), work per turn (J), heat stored each pass (J), efficiency (%), power per mass (W/kg), clock (min:s). not in the model, never say it is shown: gas burner, water jacket, pressurized gas tank, piston ring, shaft seal, speed governor, drive belt, electric generator. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=stirling"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Same temperature, no motion. Both plates are at 30 °C. Air is sealed inside, but nothing pushes on it. With no difference, the wheel sits at 0 rpm.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0 mt=100 labels=hotPlate,coldPlate"]},{"say":"Step 2: Heat one side only. Heat flows into the bottom plate from outside. After 1:30 it is 84 °C while the top stays 30 °C, and the wheel has started turning.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 speed=1 hi=hotPlate labels=hotPlate,coldPlate,air"]},{"say":"Step 3: Hot air pushes. The displacer is up high, so most of the air sits on the hot plate. Hot air presses harder: 127 kPa, enough to shove the piston up.","do":["set m view=chamber speed=0.04167 mt=4.875 hi=hotPlate,powerPiston labels=air,powerPiston"]},{"say":"Step 4: Air moves to the cold side. The displacer drops. It does not push the air out, it just moves it through the regenerator to the cold plate. Pressure falls to 111 kPa.","do":["set m hi=displacer,regenerator labels=displacer,regenerator"]},{"say":"Step 5: Cold air is easy to squeeze. The air is now cold and down to 107 kPa. The heavy flywheel keeps turning and presses the piston back down with little effort.","do":["set m hi=coldPlate,powerPiston labels=coldPlate,powerPiston"]},{"say":"Step 6: Back to the hot side. The displacer rises, air returns to the hot plate and pressure is back at 127 kPa. The push beats the squeeze, so each turn gains 0.5 J. That is the area of the loop.","do":["set m view=section hi=displacer,flywheel labels=displacer,flywheel"]}]}

name: structure-3d
desc: 3D working model: airplane wing, inside a wing, spars, ribs, stringers, fuselage, frames, fuel tank, wing bending, wing flex, load path, aircraft structure, bending moment, airliner. views: hero front wing tank root. parts: skin (Skin), spars (Spars), ribs (Ribs), stringers (Stringers), fuelTank (Fuel tank), frames (Frames), fuselageSkin (Body skin), centerBox (Center box), loadPath (Load path), liftArrows (Lift), fuelWeight (Fuel weight), bodyFuel (Fuel in the body). effects: xray explode. clock: model time is a flight in windows: 0-2 parked, 2-6 climbing, 6-16 cruise, 16-24 hardest turn (2.5 g), 24-32 strength test (3.75 g), 35-42 cruise, 42-52 what-if with the wing fuel moved to the body, 55+ cruise. Jump with mt, hold with a low speed.. shows: skin, stringers, ribs, two spars, fuel tank and center box of a wing, peeled apart (explode) or seen through (x-ray); body skin, frames every 20 in, body stringers and floor; the wing's real bend: sagging when parked, rising in cruise, more in a hard turn and most in the strength test; lift arrows above the wing and fuel-weight arrows under it, sized by local load; load paths walking along the spars into the center box and up the body frames; a what-if: the same fuel moved from the wings to the body, with the bending rising. readouts: load (g), lift (lb), wing tip rise (ft), bending at the root (million lb-ft), fuel in wings (gal), cabin pressure above outside (psi), wingspan (ft), flight weight (lb). not in the model, never say it is shown: flap, aileron, slat, spoiler, winglet, landing gear, rudder, elevator, seat, door, cockpit, fuel pump, fuel line, vent, rivet, fan blade, turbine. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=structure"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: It looks solid. It is hollow.. These wings span 117 ft, but they are not one solid piece. A thin metal skin wraps around a light frame.","do":["set m view=hero speed=0.1 mt=8 labels=skin,fuselageSkin"]},{"say":"Step 2: Skin and stringers. Lift the skin off and you find stringers: long thin strips running out toward the tip. They stop the thin skin from buckling, like the ribs on a cardboard box.","do":["set m view=wing explode=1 speed=0.1 hi=skin,stringers labels=skin,stringers"]},{"say":"Step 3: Two spars: the backbone. Two big beams run the length of the wing, one near the front and one near the back. They carry most of the bending.","do":["set m hi=spars labels=spars"]},{"say":"Step 4: 24 ribs hold the shape. Ribs are wing-shaped plates set across the spars, 24 in each wing. They keep the curve of the wing. The holes in them save weight.","do":["set m xray=0.9 explode=0 hi=ribs labels=ribs"]},{"say":"Step 5: Most of it is a fuel tank. The sealed box between the spars holds fuel: 2,600 gallons across the two wings. There is no separate tank. The wing itself is the tank.","do":["set m view=tank hi=fuelTank labels=fuelTank"]},{"say":"Step 6: Joined through the body. Both wings meet at a strong center box inside the body. Round frames every 20 in hold the body skin against 8 psi of cabin air.","do":["set m view=root hi=centerBox labels=centerBox,frames"]}]}

name: supersonic-3d
desc: 3D working model: sound barrier, sonic boom, Mach number, Mach cone, shock wave, speed of sound, swept wings, supersonic flight, transonic drag. views: close wide ground top topClose. parts: jet (Fast jet), waves (Sound waves), pileUp (Waves piled into a wall), cone (Mach cone (nose shock wave)), tailShock (Tail shock wave), listener (Listener), boomLine (Boom reaching the ground), dragArrow (Drag), sweptWing (Swept wing), straightWing (Straight wing), feltSpeed (Speed the wing feels), ground (Ground). effects: none. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second. Each flight has its own 200 s: mt 0 Mach 0.7, 200 Mach 1, 400 Mach 1.5, 600 speeding up from Mach 0.5 to 1.5 (Mach 1 at mt 630), 800 boom over a listener (jet overhead at mt 860, boom at mt 882.5), 1000 two wings at Mach 0.9, 1200 two wings at Mach 1.5. Start about 60 s into a flight so the waves have spread.. shows: sound waves leaving the nose every 2 seconds and spreading at the speed of sound; waves bunching ahead of a jet below Mach 1, piling into a wall at Mach 1, trailing in a cone above Mach 1; the jet speeding up from Mach 0.5 to 1.5 with the waves piling up live; nose and tail shock waves; the Mach cone at its true angle (42 degrees at Mach 1.5); a listener on the ground: silent as the jet passes, boom about 22 s later when the cone arrives; the boom's curved line sweeping along the ground behind the jet; drag number rising near Mach 1 (arrow length and readout); swept and straight wings side by side: the speed each wing feels, a shock on the straight wing, wingtips in or out of the cone. readouts: Mach number, speed (mph), speed of sound (mph), altitude (ft), air temperature (°F), drag number, cone angle (degrees), time since the jet passed (s), distance the jet has gone (mi), wing sweep (degrees), Mach felt by each wing. not in the model, never say it is shown: afterburner, landing gear, flap, slat, air intake, inlet, turbine, vapor cone, condensation, cockpit, pilot, variable sweep. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=supersonic"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Sound is a moving wave. A jet pushes on the air, and the push spreads out as waves, like ripples on a pond. At 30,000 ft the air is very cold and those waves travel at 678 mph.","do":["set m view=close speed=1 mt=60 hi=waves labels=waves"]},{"say":"Step 2: Slower than sound. At Mach 0.7, or 475 mph, the jet flies at 0.7 times the speed of sound. Its waves still run out ahead, bunched up, so the air gets a warning and moves aside.","do":["set m view=close speed=1 hi=jet labels=jet,waves"]},{"say":"Step 3: Mach 1: the waves can't escape. At 678 mph the jet keeps up with its own waves. Mach 1 means exactly the speed of sound. Every wave piles up at the nose into one wall of squeezed air.","do":["set m view=close speed=1 mt=260 hi=pileUp labels=pileUp"]},{"say":"Step 4: That wall is the sound barrier. The air can't move aside in time, so drag jumps. The drag number goes from 1.0 to 2.4. Early on it felt like hitting a wall, but it is only air.","do":["set m view=close speed=1 hi=dragArrow labels=dragArrow,pileUp"]},{"say":"Step 5: Pushing through. With enough push, the jet speeds up right through Mach 1.0. Watch the waves crowd together at the nose, and then get left behind.","do":["set m view=close speed=6 mt=609 hi=waves labels=waves"]},{"say":"Step 6: On the other side. At Mach 1.5, or 1,017 mph, the jet outruns its sound and the waves trail in a cone. Near the ground the warmer air carries sound faster, so Mach 1 there is 761 mph.","do":["set m view=close speed=1 mt=470 hi=cone labels=cone,jet"]}]}

name: suspension-3d
desc: 3D working model: car suspension, shock absorber, coil spring, damper, damping, spring, worn shocks, bouncing car, smooth ride, control arm, speed bump, pothole, oscillation, mass spring damper, quarter car, energy to heat. views: corner front side shock piston. parts: tire (Tire), spring (Coil spring), shock (Shock absorber), piston (Piston), oil (Oil), bumpStop (Bump stop), upperArm (Upper control arm), lowerArm (Lower control arm), knuckle (Knuckle), body (Car body), bodyPath (Path of the body), wheelPath (Path of the wheel). effects: cut xray. clock: real seconds, in 10 s windows, jump with mt; the road feature's middle reaches the axle 1 s into each window, so slow down around it: new shock bump 0-10, new shock pothole 10-20, no shock bump 20-30, no shock pothole 30-40, worn shock bump 40-50, no spring bump 50-60, no spring pothole 60-70. Numbers held on screen (moved, jolt, hardest) count from 0.4 s before the feature.. shows: one front corner of a 3,500 lb car from a real quarter-car model: 770 lb body, 90 lb wheel, 115 lb/in spring, 1,150 lb/in tire, shock 1,600 N s/m; double control arms as an exact four-bar linkage, knuckle and wheel lean, shock and spring move 0.64 of the wheel's travel; 3 in speed bump, 3 ft long, 10 mph. New shock: wheel 3.1 in, body 2.1 in, 0.8 g, 2 bounces, settled in 1.1 s, shock up to 501 lb, 234 ft-lb to heat, spring up to 1,040 lb; no shock, same bump: body 2.4 in, about 1.2 bounces a second, still bouncing at the end of the window; worn shock (20 % strength, oil leaked): 7 bounces, settled in 5.9 s, 84 ft-lb to heat; no spring: body rests 3.8 in low on the rubber bump stop; same bump throws it 4.9 in, 2.0 g, stop hit 2,224 lb; 3 in deep, 2 ft long pothole, 30 mph. New shock: wheel 1.4 in, body 0.3 in; no shock: wheel 2.3 in, body 0.3 in; no spring: body 0.5 in, 1.1 g; from the side: live paths of the body and the wheel at true height, and the road cut along the wheel's line; a real tire bridges sharp edges: the road under the wheel is a rigid 25 in circle rolled over the true road. readouts: road feature (in), speed (mph), wheel and body movement (in), hardest jolt (g), bounces, time to settle (s), spring rate (lb/in), spring load and hardest push (lb), shock strength (%), piston speed (in/s), shock hardest pull (lb), turned to heat (ft-lb), bump stop load (lb). not in the model, never say it is shown: sway bar, anti-roll bar, strut, steering, tie rod, brake, drive axle, air spring, leaf spring, gas chamber, engine, other wheels, tire pressure. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=suspension"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: The wheel is not bolted to the body. Here is one corner of a car. The wheel hangs from the body, so the wheel can jump up and down while the body stays much calmer.","do":["set m view=corner speed=0.1 mt=0 labels=tire,body"]},{"say":"Step 2: The wheel takes the hit. At 10 mph, a 3 in speed bump throws the wheel up 3.1 in, in under a fifth of a second. So far the body has risen only 1.5 in.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.08 mt=0.8 hi=tire labels=wheelPath,bodyPath"]},{"say":"Step 3: Arms swing like hinges. Two control arms join the wheel to the body. They swing up and down like door hinges, so the wheel can only move the way the bump needs it to.","do":["set m view=front speed=0.06 mt=1 hi=upperArm,lowerArm labels=upperArm,lowerArm,knuckle"]},{"say":"Step 4: The spring soaks it up. The coil spring normally holds up 770 lb. The bump squeezes it, and it pushes back as hard as 1,040 lb. It lifts the body slowly, not all at once.","do":["set m view=corner speed=0.08 mt=1.02 hi=spring labels=spring"]},{"say":"Step 5: Then it calms down. The body moved 2.1 in, less than the wheel, and far more gently. The shock absorber stops the rest: 2 small bounces, and all quiet 1.1 s after the bump.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.35 mt=1.3 hi= labels=wheelPath,bodyPath"]},{"say":"Step 6: A pothole at 30 mph. The tire drops 1.4 in into a 3 in pothole and hits the far edge, while the body moves just 0.3 in. That gap between wheel and body is the smooth ride.","do":["set m view=side xray=0 speed=0.06 mt=10.91 hi=tire labels=tire"]},{"say":"Step 7: Now take the spring away. With no spring, the body rests on a rubber stop. The same bump throws it 4.9 in with a 2.0 g jolt. With the spring, it was 2.1 in and 0.8 g.","do":["set m view=side xray=0.8 speed=0.2 mt=50.92 hi= labels=bodyPath,bumpStop"]}]}

name: telescope-3d
desc: 3D working model: space telescope, telescope, infrared telescope, reflecting telescope, curved mirror, parabolic mirror, mirror segments, light gathering, collecting area, focal point, detector, reflection, why telescopes go to space, atmosphere blocks infrared, twinkling stars, atmospheric blur, resolution, sunshield, multi-layer insulation, radiation heat transfer, infrared and heat, Wien's law, Sun-Earth far point. views: wide mirror inside shield mountain. parts: primaryMirror (First mirror), secondaryMirror (Second mirror), instruments (Instruments), detector (Detector), sunshield (Five-layer sunshield), solarPanel (Solar panel), lightRays (Starlight), sun (Sun), earth (Earth), moon (Moon), mountain (Telescope on a mountain), air (Air). effects: xray explode. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: starlight 0-60 (rays reach the detector over the first 6 s, light slowed), mountain beside the telescope 60-110, Sun on the shield with heat leaving the gaps 110-130 (arrows from 114), same with shield size on the panel 130-140, warm mirror 140-146, cooling 146-176 (1 s = 5 days), cold 176-180. shows: 18 gold hexagon segments on one curved bowl, a second mirror on three legs, a hole in the middle, a box of instruments behind it with a third mirror and a detector inside (x-ray); By the time it arrives, the rays run side by side, and only the rays that land on the mirror count.","do":["set m view=wide speed=1 mt=0 hi=lightRays labels=lightRays"]},{"say":"Step 2: A giant golden bowl. 18 hexagon pieces fit together into one curved mirror 6.5 m wide. A gold layer, only about 49 g in all, bounces infrared light very well.","do":["set m view=mirror hi=primaryMirror labels=primaryMirror"]},{"say":"Step 3: A bigger bucket for light. Think of a bucket in the rain. This one has 25.4 m² of mirror, so it catches about 660,000 times as much light as the pupil of your eye.","do":["set m view=mirror hi=primaryMirror,lightRays labels=primaryMirror"]},{"say":"Step 4: The curve aims every ray. The bowl shape sends all the rays toward one spot. On the way they hit a second mirror, just 0.74 m wide, held 7.2 m out in front.","do":["set m view=inside xray=0 hi=secondaryMirror labels=secondaryMirror"]},{"say":"Step 5: Down the hole to the detector. name: tiltrotor-3d
desc: 3D working model: tilt-rotor, VTOL, hover, conversion, transition to forward flight, nacelle, rotor, lift, thrust, wing lift, cross-shaft, engine failure, retreating blade stall, advancing blade, helicopter top speed. views: side threeq front top shaft. parts: rotors (Rotors), nacelles (Tilting nacelles), leftEngine (Left engine), rightEngine (Right engine), crossShaft (Cross-shaft), wing (Wing), rotorLift (Rotor lift), thrust (Thrust), wingLift (Wing lift), weight (Weight), fastSide (Fast side), slowSide (Slow side). effects: xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second (rotors drawn slowly, rpm on screen is true); the job moving from rotors to wing as speed builds (wing carries all 16,800 lb from about 190 mph); air through each rotor, straight down in a hover, swept back at speed; a color map of air speed over the rotor circle, fast side and slow side, and a stall zone growing on the slow side; blade tip speeds: fast side, slow side, the speed of sound, and how close the slow blade is to stalling (limit at 150 mph held up, about 10% at 300 mph tipped forward); x-ray: both engines, the one-way clutch, gearboxes and the cross-shaft running along the tilt axis inside the wing; The nacelles turn slowly, here to 79°. The rotors now only need 11,800 lb of lift, so they can tip further, to 61°.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=0.5 mt=26 hi=wing,wingLift labels=wingLift,rotorLift,thrust"]},{"say":"Step 4: The job swaps over. At 120 mph the wing carries 12,400 lb and the rotors only 4,400 lb. The nacelles are down to 30° and more of the pull goes into thrust.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 mt=32 hi=wingLift,thrust labels=wingLift,thrust"]},{"say":"Step 5: Now it is a plane. At 0° the rotors are big propellers.
