name: trainwheel-3d
desc: 3D working model: train wheels, coned wheel tread, wheelset, flange, how trains stay on the track, how trains turn, self-centering, sway wavelength, rolling radius, track switch, turnout, points, frog, train air brake, brake pipe, brake shoes. views: front top points turnout brakes. parts: tread (Coned tread), flange (Flange), axle (Solid axle), rail (Rail), wavePath (Path of the axle), points (Point rails), switchMachine (Switch machine), frog (Frog and guard rails), brakePipe (Brake pipe), valve (Control valve), reservoir (Air tank), shoes (Brake shoes). effects: xray. clock: fixed windows (mt): 0 axle swaying back to center at 60 mph, 30 hard shove until the flange touches, 50 straight then gentle 3,000 ft curve (curve starts at 62), 75 straight then tight 600 ft curve (curve starts at 81), 100 car runs the straight way, 115 points move, 122 car runs the turnout way, 140 air brake (pipe cut at 146-156, held to 163, released by 169). Rolling scenes run at 1/8 speed; on the wheelset the side shift is drawn 6 times larger, the cone 4 times steeper, and curves far tighter.. shows: a solid axle with two coned wheels rolling on rails, flanges clear of the rail; the axle drifting right, right wheel rolling on a bigger radius, the axle steering itself back in a 54 ft wave; a hard shove closing the 0.375 in play until the flange touches the rail; the axle shifting 0.30 in outward on a 3,000 ft curve so the outer wheel rolls farther each turn; a 600 ft curve needing more shift than the flange allows, flange on the rail and wheels slipping; a turnout: two point rails tied together, moved 4.75 in by a switch machine, the closed point steering the flange, the frog and guard rails; a rail car taking either route; air brake on one car: pipe pressure cut from 90 psi, tank air going to the cylinder, shoes pressing the wheels, release. readouts: speed (mph), wheel radius (in), side shift (in), flange gap (in), tread slope, sway wave (ft), curve radius (ft), extra rail length (ft), slip (ft), point travel (in), point rail length (ft), frog slope, pipe, tank, cylinder pressure (psi), cylinder push and shoe force (lb). not in the model, never say it is shown: spring, bearing, coupler, signal, superelevation, locomotive, emergency reservoir, slack adjuster, handbrake, hand brake, engineer, dynamic brake, detector, bolt, tie plate, spike. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=trainwheel"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Not the flanges. Most people guess the rims hold the train on. They are only the backup. The real work is done by the tread, which is a cone with a slope of 1 in 20. Here it is drawn steeper so you can see it.","do":["set m view=front speed=0.5 mt=8 hi=tread labels=tread,flange"]},{"say":"Step 2: The axle drifts right. Say the axle slides 0.30 in to the right. The right wheel now rolls on its wider part, 18.015 in radius. The left rolls on its narrower part, 17.985 in.","do":["set m view=front speed=0.02 mt=0 hi=tread labels=tread"]},{"say":"Step 3: One solid axle. Both wheels are fixed to one axle, so they turn at the same rate. The wider wheel covers more ground each turn, so the axle steers itself back toward the middle.","do":["set m view=top speed=0.5 mt=0.4 hi=axle labels=axle"]},{"say":"Step 4: It settles by itself. It overshoots a little and steers back again, one gentle wave every 54 ft, at 60 mph. Friction calms the wave. The orange path is drawn much wider than real.","do":["set m view=top speed=1 hi=wavePath labels=wavePath"]},{"say":"Step 5: Flanges are the backup. There is only 0.375 in of play each way. A hard shove closes it, and the flange touches the rail and stops the slide. On straight track that is rare.","do":["set m view=front speed=0.5 mt=33.5 hi=flange labels=flange,rail"]}]}

name: turbo-3d
desc: 3D working model: turbocharger, turbo, boost, turbo lag, intercooler, wastegate, compressor wheel, exhaust turbine, forced induction, car engine power. views: full outside turbo cooler gate. parts: turbine (Exhaust turbine), compressor (Compressor wheel), shaft (Shaft), wastegate (Wastegate), intercooler (Intercooler), intakePipe (Intake pipe), engine (Engine), exhaustPipe (Exhaust pipe), intakeAir (Air going in), exhaustGas (Exhaust gas), coolAir (Outside air). effects: cut xray. clock: steady windows: 0-100 full boost, 100-200 no boost, 200-300 full boost with no cooling (1 model second = 1 rotor turn on screen). 300-320 lag run at 3,000 rpm with the pedal down at 301 (1 model second = 1 real second; run it slowly with speed). shows: exhaust from the engine spinning the turbine, shaft turning the compressor wheel; air packed tighter after the compressor (dots bunch up) and how much hotter it gets; intercooler: dots change from amber to pale blue through the fins, outside air blowing across; wastegate door sending part of the exhaust around the turbine to hold boost at the limit; turbo lag: pedal down, rotor speed and boost climbing over about 1.5 seconds, power following; power compared: no boost, full boost, full boost with no cooling. readouts: power (hp), boost (psi), rotor speed (rpm), engine speed (rpm), air temperatures (°F), exhaust temperature (°F), air packed (× outside), wastegate opening (%), shaft power (hp), gas pedal (%), time after pedal (s). not in the model, never say it is shown: air filter, blow-off, throttle, fuel injector, injector, spark plug, oil line, coolant, radiator, catalytic converter, muffler, belt, timing chain, boost hose, sensor, flywheel, transmission. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=turbo"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: An engine runs on air. Burning gas needs air. With no boost, this 2.0 liter engine only gets the air that outside pressure pushes in, and it makes about 120 hp at 5,000 rpm.","do":["set m view=full cut=1 speed=0.6 mt=100 hi=engine labels=engine,intakeAir"]},{"say":"Step 2: Exhaust spins a wheel. Exhaust leaves the engine at about 1,650 °F, normally wasted. Here it first rushes through a turbine and spins it at about 150,000 rpm.","do":["set m view=turbo speed=0.7 mt=0 hi=turbine,exhaustGas labels=turbine,exhaustGas"]},{"say":"Step 3: A shaft joins two wheels. The turbine and the compressor wheel sit on one short shaft. Exhaust energy crosses to the air side, about 22 hp of it, with no link to the engine's crank.","do":["set m view=turbo speed=0.7 hi=shaft labels=shaft,turbine,compressor"]},{"say":"Step 4: The other wheel packs in air. The compressor wheel flings air outward and squeezes it to 15 psi above outside pressure. See the dots bunch up: the air is getting crowded.","do":["set m view=turbo speed=0.7 hi=compressor,intakeAir labels=compressor,intakeAir"]},{"say":"Step 5: More air, more fuel, more power. Each cylinder now takes in 1.9 times as much air, so it can burn 1.9 times the fuel. Same engine: about 220 hp instead of 120 hp.","do":["set m view=full speed=0.7 hi=engine,intakePipe labels=engine,intakePipe,intercooler"]},{"say":"Step 6: A door keeps it safe. Too much boost could hurt the engine. The wastegate is a door that lets about 30% of the exhaust skip the turbine, which holds boost at 15 psi.","do":["set m view=gate speed=0.6 hi=wastegate labels=wastegate,exhaustGas"]}]}

name: turboprop-3d
desc: 3D working model: turboprop, propeller engine, reduction gearbox, variable pitch, propeller blade angle, turboprop vs turbofan, regional airplane, gas turbine, free power turbine, torque and rpm, speed of sound at the blade tip. views: front side core gearbox compare. parts: propeller (Propeller), pitch (Blade-angle piston), gearbox (Reduction gearbox), compressor (Compressor), combustor (Combustion chamber), gasTurbine (Turbine 1 (runs compressor)), powerTurbine (Turbine 2 (power turbine)), exhaust (Exhaust), powerShaft (Power shaft), propAir (Air thrown by the propeller), coreAir (Air into the engine), turbofan (Turbofan, same scale). effects: cut. clock: 1 model second = 1 propeller turn at 1,200 rpm; mt windows pick the flight: 0 takeoff, 200 cruise with blade-angle change, 300 cruise beside a turbofan, 400 at 530 mph with tips past the speed of sound, 500 trip times, 600 what if no gearbox (propeller at turbine speed). shows: air through a scoop under the nose into the compressor, squeezed, burned, through two turbines and out of the exhaust; first turbine drives the compressor; free second turbine drives the power shaft to the gearbox; two-stage reduction gears: small gear on big gear (offset), then planetary with fixed ring; 20,000 to 4,800 to 1,200 rpm, torque rising to match; six-blade propeller whose blades twist on their roots (18 degrees at takeoff, 38 in cruise) moved by a sliding piston in the hub; the propeller moves far more air than the core: about 1,200 lb/s against 15 lb/s; 8,700 lb from the propeller, 230 lb from the exhaust; a same-scale turbofan beside the propeller; efficiency crossover at 345 mph and 530 mph; blade tips past the speed of sound; trip times for 300 and 1,500 miles. readouts: power (hp), thrust (lb), propeller, turbine and core speed (rpm), gear ratio, torque (lb-ft), tip speed and speed of sound (mph), blade angle (degrees), pressure (psi), temperatures (°F), air and fuel flow (lb/s), flight speed (mph), altitude (ft), efficiency (%), trip time. not in the model, never say it is shown: landing gear, oil cooler, starter, generator, igniter, de-icing, propeller brake, thrust reverser, flap, aileron, fuselage, fuel tank, fuel pump. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=turboprop"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A jet engine that spins a propeller. Inside the pod on the wing is a small jet engine. Its main job is to turn this 13 ft propeller with 2,500 hp.","do":["set m view=front speed=0.15 mt=0 labels=propeller"]},{"say":"Step 2: Squeeze. A little air enters a scoop under the nose. Spinning compressor blades squeeze it to 15 times normal pressure, and that heats it to about 800 °F.","do":["set m view=side cut=1 speed=0.1 hi=compressor labels=compressor,coreAir"]},{"say":"Step 3: Burn. Fuel burns non-stop in the squeezed air, about 0.28 lb every second. The gas comes out at about 2,100 °F.","do":["set m view=core speed=0.06 hi=combustor labels=combustor"]},{"say":"Step 4: Spin two turbines. The first turbine keeps the compressor going at 30,000 rpm. The second is free to turn on its own at 20,000 rpm, and it drives the propeller.","do":["set m view=core speed=0.05 hi=gasTurbine,powerTurbine labels=gasTurbine,powerTurbine"]},{"say":"Step 5: Slow it down. A long shaft carries that spin forward to a gearbox. The gears bring 20,000 rpm down to 1,200 rpm for the propeller.","do":["set m view=gearbox speed=0.1 hi=powerShaft,gearbox labels=powerShaft,gearbox"]},{"say":"Step 6: Throw air back. The propeller throws about 1,200 lb of air back each second. That gives 8,700 lb of push. The exhaust adds only 230 lb.","do":["set m view=side cut=0 speed=0.15 hi=propeller,propAir labels=propeller,propAir,exhaust"]},{"say":"Step 7: Blades that twist. A piston in the hub twists every blade on its root, from 18° for takeoff to 38° for cruise, so each bite of air suits the speed.","do":["set m view=gearbox cut=1 speed=0.12 mt=200 hi=pitch labels=pitch,propeller"]}]}

name: ujoint-3d
desc: 3D working model: driveshaft, drive shaft, universal joint, u-joint, slip yoke, cv joint, constant velocity joint, half-shaft, axle shaft, rear-wheel drive, front-wheel drive, speed wobble, driveshaft vibration, yoke phasing, steering joint. views: side rear slip axle cv. parts: transmission (Transmission), slipYoke (Slip yoke), frontJoint (Front U-joint), driveshaft (Driveshaft), rearJoint (Rear U-joint), rearAxle (Rear axle), cvJoint (CV joint), cvBalls (Steel balls), halfShaft (Half-shaft), frontWheel (Front wheel), testJoint (Single U-joint), chart (Speed chart). effects: cut. clock: 8× slow motion (shaft 2.08 turns a model second at speed 1). Fixed windows, jump with mt: road 0-40 (axle ±3 in, period 8; peak up at 2, 10, 18, 26, 34), axle held up 3 in 40-60, same with the rear fork turned 90° 60-80, front axle straight 80-84, steering in 84-87, held 30° 87-140.. shows: rear-drive driveline: transmission tail, splined output, slip yoke, front U-joint, 50 in driveshaft, rear U-joint, rear axle on two parallel links and coil springs; all joint angles from the exact rule that the two pins of a cross stay square: joint angle 1° to 6° as the axle moves ±3 in, slip yoke slides 1.6 in end to end; at 6°: transmission steady 1,000 rpm, driveshaft 995 to 1,006 rpm, axle input steady 1,000 rpm, the same angle at every instant; the rear fork turned 90° on the shaft: axle input 989 to 1,011 rpm; front axle, 282 rpm at 22 mph, steered to 30°: left half a CV joint, the other half a single U-joint for comparison; the U-joint's wheel 244 to 325 rpm, two hills a turn, the CV wheel steady at 282; ball-type CV joint cut open: 6 balls in a cage, inner part and outer bell with grooves, balls in the plane halving the angle (15° at 30° steering), good to 45°; live chart of speed over one turn, with a dot for each shaft. readouts: transmission, driveshaft, axle input rpm, joint angle (°), axle moved (in), slip yoke slide (in), car speed (mph), low and high rpm, steering (°), half-shaft rpm, wheel rpm, ball plane (°), balls. not in the model, never say it is shown: engine, clutch, differential gears, ring gear, center support bearing, two-piece driveshaft, shock absorber, front suspension, control arm, steering rack, tie rod, brake, rubber boot, plunging inner joint, tripod, car body, front wheels of the rear-drive car. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=ujoint"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Two ends that don't line up. The transmission is bolted to the car. The rear axle rides on springs and moves with the road. A long shaft has to carry the turning from one to the other, here at 1,000 rpm at 22 mph.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 mt=0.5 labels=transmission,driveshaft,rearAxle"]},{"say":"Step 2: The axle goes up and down. Over this bump the axle has moved up 3 in while the transmission stays put. A solid straight shaft would bend or break.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.5 mt=8.5 hi=rearAxle labels=rearAxle,driveshaft"]},{"say":"Step 3: A U-joint is a spinning hinge. Two forks grab a small cross, each fork on its own pair of arms. The joint can bend and keep turning. Here the shaft meets the axle at a 6° angle.","do":["set m view=rear speed=0.1 mt=9.65 hi=rearJoint labels=rearJoint"]},{"say":"Step 4: The slip yoke lets it stretch. The axle swings on links, so the gap to the transmission keeps changing. The slip yoke slides on grooves that still pass the turning, up to 1.6 in end to end.","do":["set m view=slip speed=0.5 mt=16.4 hi=slipYoke labels=slipYoke,frontJoint,transmission"]},{"say":"Step 5: Bend, slide and keep turning. Two U-joints handle the bending and the slip yoke handles the length, so the shaft never stops turning, whatever the road does.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.6 mt=24 hi= labels=frontJoint,rearJoint"]}]}

name: v8-3d
desc: 3D working model: V8 engine, V engine, firing order, cross-plane crankshaft, crankshaft, pistons, camshaft, timing chain, V6 vs V8, pickup truck engine, car engine. views: threeq front side top chain. parts: block (Engine block), piston (Piston), rod (Connecting rod), crank (Crankshaft), camshaft (Camshaft), timingChain (Timing chain), valve (Valves), sparkPlug (Spark plug), numbers (Cylinder numbers), vAngle (90° V), rowGhost (One row of 8), compare (V8 vs V6 numbers). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = one firing (90° of crank); one full cycle = 8 s. shows: 8 pistons on a cross-plane crank, each from the exact slider-crank; firing order 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2: numbered cylinders, spark and burn in the right cylinder at the right angle; four strokes in cylinders 1 and 2 with the block cut open; the 90° V, two rods sharing each crankpin; a timing chain driving four camshafts at half crank speed, four valves per cylinder; how long the same 8 cylinders would be in one straight row; V8 and V6 numbers side by side (the V6 is numbers only, it is not on screen). readouts: crank angle, cylinder 1 stroke and pressure (psi), firing now, next, fires per second at 2,000 rpm, size (cu in), power (hp), torque (lb-ft), row length (in), V angle, V6 numbers. not in the model, never say it is shown: intake manifold, exhaust manifold, manifold, flywheel, transmission, water pump, radiator, alternator, oil pump, oil filter, fuel injector, injector, throttle, timing cover, turbo, pushrod, intake port, exhaust port, muffler. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=v8"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Eight cylinders, one crankshaft. This is a pickup-truck V8. It has 302 cubic inches of cylinders and makes 395 hp and 400 lb-ft of torque.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=1.2 mt=0 labels=block,timingChain,sparkPlug"]},{"say":"Step 2: Each cylinder does 4 strokes. Suck in air and gas. Squeeze it. Burn it, which shoves the piston down. Push the exhaust out. Only the burn makes power.","do":["set m view=front cut=1 speed=1 mt=4 hi= labels=piston,rod,sparkPlug"]},{"say":"Step 3: Up-and-down becomes round-and-round. Each piston pushes on a rod, and the rod turns the crankshaft, like your leg turning a bicycle pedal.","do":["set m view=side cut=0 xray=1 speed=0.8 hi=crank labels=crank,piston"]},{"say":"Step 4: Why a V: it is short. Eight cylinders in one straight row would be 31 in long. Two rows of 4 are only 17 in, so it fits under a hood.","do":["set m view=side xray=0 speed=0.4 hi=rowGhost labels=rowGhost"]},{"say":"Step 5: Two rows, 90° apart. The rows lean apart by 90°, and each pair of rods shares one crank pin. So the crankshaft stays short and stiff too.","do":["set m view=front xray=1 speed=0.4 hi=vAngle labels=vAngle,rod"]},{"say":"Step 6: Chains keep it all in time. Timing chains spin the camshafts at half the crank's speed. The cams open each valve at just the right moment.","do":["set m view=chain xray=0 speed=0.8 hi=camshaft,timingChain labels=timingChain,camshaft"]}]}

name: vibration-3d
desc: 3D working model: vibration, natural frequency, resonance, spring-mass-damper, damping, frequency response, shaker table, wheel balance, unbalanced wheel, centripetal force, tuned mass damper, tall building sway, wind sway. views: bench coil wheel tower top. parts: shaker (Shaker table), mass (Mass), spring (Spring), damper (Damper), curve (Response curve), wheel (Wheel), heavySpot (Heavy spot), balanceWeight (Balance weight), hubMount (Spring mount), tower (Tower), tunedMass (Tuned mass), tmdLinks (Cables and dampers). effects: none. clock: bench, 1 model s = 1/4 real s: 0-25 sweep 2-12 Hz (0.4 Hz per model s), 25-35 hold 5.03 Hz, 35-41 hold 2 Hz, 41-47 hold 10 Hz, 47-59 let go with table off, 59-74 8 kg sweep 1-7 Hz, 74-84 hold 2.52 Hz. Wheel, 1 model s = 1/16 real s: 90-100 15 m/s, 100-110 30 m/s, 110-126 sweep 5-35 m/s, 126-136 hold 24.75 m/s, 136-146 same with the balance weight going on over 1 s. Tower, 1 model s = 4 real s: 150-250 mass locked until 156 then free, settled by about 225; 260-400 cables 6.6 m, free at 262, settled by about 385. Jump with mt. shows: a 2.0 kg mass on a 2,000 N/m spring and 6.3 N·s/m damper on a shaker table moving 3 mm each way, natural frequency 5.03 Hz; a live sweep drawing mass movement against table frequency on a chart: 3.6 mm at 2 Hz, 30.3 mm at 5.03 Hz, 1.0 mm at 10 Hz; the mass let go with the table off: it bobs at 5.03 Hz, dying away; 8.0 kg (3 extra plates, damper 12.6 N·s/m): the peak moves to 2.52 Hz, same 30.3 mm; a 40 kg wheel with a 0.040 kg heavy spot at 0.20 m, a rotating arrow to scale for the pull on the axle: 16.5 N at 15 m/s, 66.1 N at 30 m/s; wheel in a 225,000 N/m spring mount: natural frequency 11.9 Hz, worst at 24.8 m/s, hub shake 0.50 mm, drawn 60 times real size; a 0.040 kg balance weight clipped opposite: pull 0 N, hub still, static balance only; a 400 m tower, 0.15 Hz, wind push 216 kN in rhythm, top sway 300 mm with the mass locked, 50 mm free (worst wind beat 59 mm), drawn 100 times real size; a 600,000 kg mass (1.5% of the moving mass) on 11.2 m cables with dampers, swinging 339 mm, pull 180 kN, drawn 14 times real size; shorter 6.6 m cables mistune it: 181 mm sway. readouts: frequency (Hz), movement (mm), mass (kg), stiffness (N/m), damping (N·s/m), road speed (m/s), pull (N, kN), cable length (m). not in the model, never say it is shown: road drum, suspension arm, steering wheel, brake, bridge, soldier, elevator, earthquake, accelerometer, second plane. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=vibration"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Every spring-mass has its own beat. Lift this 2.0 kg mass on its 2,000 N/m spring and let go. It bobs 5.03 times a second. That is its natural frequency.","do":["set m view=bench speed=0.7 mt=47 hi=mass,spring labels=mass,spring"]},{"say":"Step 2: Shake it slowly. Now the table shakes the spring 2 times a second, moving 3 mm each way. The mass just rides along, moving 3.6 mm.","do":["set m speed=1 mt=35 hi=shaker labels=shaker"]},{"say":"Step 3: Speed the table up. The table keeps moving the same 3 mm, but the mass moves more and more as the table's beat gets close to the mass's own beat.","do":["set m speed=1.25 mt=0 hi=curve labels=curve"]},{"say":"Step 4: At 5.03 Hz it moves most. The same 3 mm of table now moves the mass 30.3 mm, 10 times as far. Each small push arrives just as the mass is heading that way, so each one adds energy.","do":["set m view=coil speed=1 mt=25 hi=mass labels=mass"]},{"say":"Step 5: Why it stops at 30.3 mm. The damper soaks up energy as the mass moves. The swing grows until the damper takes out as much as the table puts in.","do":["set m speed=1 mt=28 hi=damper labels=damper"]},{"say":"Step 6: Too fast, and it can't follow. At 10 Hz the mass moves only 1.0 mm, less than the table's 3 mm. It is too heavy to keep up.","do":["set m view=bench speed=1 mt=41 hi=curve labels=curve"]},{"say":"Step 7: Change the mass, move the peak. Make it 8.0 kg, four times the mass, and the peak moves to half the frequency: 2.52 Hz. Mass and stiffness set the beat.","do":["set m speed=1 mt=74 hi=mass,curve labels=mass,curve"]}]}

name: washer-3d

Weld with flux 0-110: rod lowers 0-1, touches 1-1.4, arc from 1.5, travels 2-74 (arc passes the middle, x = 0, at t 38), rod lifts away 74-78, slag comes off 84-90. Same weld with a bare rod 110-220 (add 110). Jump with mt. shows: two 1/4 in steel plates with a V between them, a power supply, cables, clamp and a rod in its holder; electrons running round the whole loop (hi cables), and the rod touching the plate then lifting 1/8 in to start the arc (t 1-2); the arc close up: blue electrons rising, orange charged gas atoms falling; the weld pool, its real teardrop size from the heat-flow math, turning solid behind the arc into a rippled bead; heat in the plate as calm tan and amber shades, fading after the arc stops; flux coating (x-ray makes coating and slag see-through), gas shield over the pool, slag crust on the bead; air dots (hi air) pushed aside by the shield; with the bare rod they reach the pool; cut-through at x = 1.2: plates, a dashed line where the plate edges used to be, weld metal, the band the heat changed; the bare-rod weld shows tiny holes. readouts: current (A), voltage (V), power (W), arc length (in), arc and melting temperatures (°F), pool length (in), seconds liquid, travel and rod melting (in/min), plate thickness, bead width (in), strength (psi), air nitrogen and oxygen (%), nitrogen and oxygen in the weld (%). not in the model, never say it is shown: helmet, glove, chipping hammer, wire brush, spatter, tack, gas cylinder, gas bottle, wire feed, MIG, TIG, transformer, fan, second pass. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=welding"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: No glue, no bolts. Welding turns two pieces of steel into one piece. It melts them where they meet. These two plates are 1/4 in thick, and the power supply sends 120 amps to do the melting.","do":["set m view=whole speed=1 mt=30 labels=plates,supply,cables"]},{"say":"Step 2: A small pool of liquid steel. An electric arc melts the edge of each plate. The two edges run together into one pool, at about 3,000 °F. Steel melts at 2,750 °F.","do":["set m view=joint speed=1 mt=34 hi=pool labels=arc,pool,plates"]},{"say":"Step 3: The rod adds new steel. The steel rod melts too, 9 in every minute, and drips into the pool. It fills the V between the plates while the arc moves along at 5 in a minute.","do":["set m view=arc xray=0.8 speed=0.6 mt=36 hi=electrode labels=electrode,pool"]},{"say":"Step 4: It freezes behind the arc. The pool is only 0.24 in long, and any spot stays liquid for about 2.9 seconds. Then it freezes into a ridge called the weld bead. Here it runs 3 times too fast.","do":["set m view=joint xray=0 speed=3 mt=42 hi=bead labels=pool,bead"]},{"say":"Step 5: Cut through: one piece. The dashed line shows where the plate edges used to be. Metal crystals grew right across it, so no seam is left. The weld holds 70,000 psi, more than the plate's 58,000 psi.","do":["set m view=section cut=1 speed=0 mt=100 hi=joint labels=joint,bead,plates"]}]}

name: wellpump-3d
desc: 3D working model: hand pump, well, suction limit, air pressure, check valve, submersible pump, pressure tank, water tower, water pressure, head. views: pump shallow deep tank tower. parts: handle (Handle), piston (Piston), pistonValve (Check valve in the piston), footValve (Lower check valve), airPush (Air pressing on the water), emptyGap (Nearly empty pipe), submersible (Submersible pump), pressureTank (Pressure tank), tower (Water tower), main (Water main), townPump (Town pump), house (Kitchen tap). effects: cut. clock: stretches by mt: 0-100 hand pump, starts with an empty pipe (1 model second = 1 s; pipe is full and spout runs from 30); 100-200 deeper well, sped up, at the limit from about 130; 200-300 tower steady; 300+ tower's day (1 model second = 1 hour from 6 AM); the pressure tank runs throughout (pump on for the first 21.7 s of each 54.1 s). shows: handle, piston and two check valves working on up and down strokes, with water moving only on the up stroke; strokes taking air out of the pipe so air pressure on the well pushes water up, 20 ft well; the same pump on a 50 ft well: water stops at 34 ft however long you pump, nearly empty pipe above; submersible pump 110 ft down pushing water up from below, into a pressure tank that holds air; water tower: height gives pressure, 0.43 psi per ft, 130 ft = 56 psi at a kitchen tap; a town's day: breakfast demand above what pumps give, tower covers the gap, refills at night. readouts: strokes per minute, gallons per stroke, flow (gpm), water depth and climb (ft), air pressure (psi), tank pressure (psi) and water (gal), tower water (gal), water height (ft), tap pressure (psi), town use and pump flow (gpm), clock. not in the model, never say it is shown: vent, power cable, pressure switch, water treatment, priming water, screen, sewer, water meter, foot valve, overflow. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=wellpump"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A handle moves a piston. Push the long handle down and a piston inside the pump rises. Water is 20 ft below, and this pump gives about 5.5 gallons per minute.","do":["set m view=pump speed=0.5 mt=40 labels=handle,piston"]},{"say":"Step 2: Piston up: water follows. As the piston rises, it leaves low pressure under it. Water pushes open the lower check valve, a flap that opens only upward, and follows the piston up.","do":["set m view=pump cut=1 speed=0.17 mt=42 hi=footValve,piston labels=footValve,piston"]},{"say":"Step 3: Piston down: water stays. When the piston drops, the lower flap slams shut so water can't fall back. A second flap in the piston opens, and the piston slides down through the water.","do":["set m view=pump speed=0.17 mt=43 hi=pistonValve labels=pistonValve,footValve"]},{"say":"Step 4: Each stroke tips some out. Now water sits above the piston too. The next rise lifts it to the spout, about 0.18 gallons per stroke. At 30 strokes a minute, that is 5.5 gallons per minute.","do":["set m view=pump speed=0.5 mt=45 hi=piston labels=piston"]},{"say":"Step 5: The first strokes pump air. A dry pipe holds only air. Each stroke takes some out, and the air pressing on the well, 14.7 psi, pushes water up the pipe to fill the space.","do":["set m view=shallow cut=0 speed=3.4 mt=0 hi=airPush labels=airPush"]}]}

name: windtunnel-3d
desc: 3D working model: wind tunnel, angle of attack, lift, stall, drag, airfoil, streamlining, pressure, boundary layer separation, aerodynamic shape. views: overview section airfoil balance gauges. parts: fan (Fan), contraction (Contraction), testSection (Test section), diffuser (Diffuser), airfoil (Airfoil), balance (Force balance), angleDial (Angle of attack), smoke (Smoke lines), pressureTaps (Pressure taps), manometer (Water columns), lift (Lift), drag (Drag). effects: xray. clock: fixed test program, jump with mt, fan and smoke in slow motion. Holds: 0° 0-10, 5° 15-25, 10° 30-40, 13° 43-53, 18° 58-68, back to 5° 74-84; wing at 0° 84-94, round bar 94-104, flat plate 104-114, wing 114-124. shows: air pulled through a 9:1 contraction into a 0.6 m test section at a steady 30 m/s by a fan at the far end; airfoil tilting from 0° to 18° on an angle scale, lift rising in a straight line to 10°, peak 112 N at 13°, falling to 74 N at 18°; five smoke lines: smooth and turned downward when attached, tearing off the top with tumbling curls in the stall; drag rising from 0.8 N to 14.4 N with angle; lift and drag arrows on the wing (drag arrow drawn 5 times the lift scale); 12 pressure taps feeding 12 water columns at true height; top-of-wing suction collapsing in the stall; swap of the test piece: same 30 mm height as wing, round bar and flat plate, with 0.8, 11.9 and 19.6 N of drag and their wakes; force balance under the floor with separate lift and drag cells; x-ray shows the fan through the duct. readouts: angle (°), lift (N), drag (N), air speed (m/s), inlet speed (m/s), air moved (m³/s), fan speed (rpm), surface pressure against the room (Pa), shape height (mm). not in the model, never say it is shown: pitot tube, turbulence screen, control room, computer, speed controller, flap, slat, turntable, wall correction. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=windtunnel"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A wing in a steady wind. A fan pulls air through this tunnel. The funnel squeezes it, so it races through the test section at 30 m/s, about highway speed.","do":["set m view=overview xray=0.8 mt=2 hi=fan labels=fan,contraction,testSection"]},{"say":"Step 2: The tilt against the air. Angle of attack is how far a wing is tipped against the air coming at it. Right now it is 0°, and this curved wing already makes 16.5 N of lift.","do":["set m view=section xray=0 mt=4 hi=angleDial labels=airfoil,angleDial"]},{"say":"Step 3: Tip it to 5°. Now the nose is up 5°. Lift jumps to 58 N. The fan has not changed. Only the angle has.","do":["set m mt=12 hi=angleDial,lift labels=angleDial,lift"]},{"say":"Step 4: It turns the air down. At 10° lift is 99 N. See the smoke bend downward behind the wing. The wing pushes air down, and the air pushes the wing up.","do":["set m view=airfoil mt=27 hi=lift,smoke labels=lift,smoke"]},{"say":"Step 5: Only up to a point. Up to 10°, each degree adds about 8 N. Then it levels off. At 13° lift tops out at 112 N. Tip it further and lift drops.","do":["set m view=section mt=41 hi=lift,angleDial labels=lift,angleDial"]}]}

name: windturbine-3d
desc: 3D working model: wind turbine, wind power, wind energy, renewable energy, electricity, generator, gearbox, blades, rotor, blade pitch, feathering, yaw, Betz limit, power coefficient, swept area, storm, kinetic energy, magnets, coils, electromagnetic induction. views: front side nacelle hub top generator rotor bladeFace. parts: tower (Tower), nacelle (Nacelle), hub (Hub), blades (Blades), pitchBearings (Pitch bearings), mainShaft (Main shaft (slow)), gearbox (Gearbox + fast shaft), generator (Generator), magnets (Magnets (spin)), coils (Copper coils (still)), yawDrive (Yaw drive), anemometer (Wind meter and vane), wind (Wind), sweptArea (Swept area), rpmGauge (Rotor speed). effects: cut xray. clock: 1 model second = 1 real second; fixed windows, jump with mt: low wind 0-20, yaw 20-58, rated + gust 60-90, storm 90-160 (cut-out at 100.3, parked by 115, yaws back 119-159). shows: a 2 MW three-blade turbine: 260 ft tower, rotor 295 ft across (145 ft blades), nacelle with cover that cuts away or x-rays; wind streaks slowing through the rotor (actuator disc): 16 mph in, 13 mph at the blades, 11 mph behind; streaks pass straight when parked; low wind 16 mph: rotor 11.9 rpm, generator 1,188 rpm, 588 kW of 1.34 MW in the wind, power coefficient 44 % vs Betz 59 %; yaw window: wind swings 15° at 21-23 s, yaw motors turn the nacelle 0.5°/s from 26 s, facing it by 56 s; wind vane shows the error; rated 25 mph: rotor 16 rpm, gearbox 100 : 1 (3 visible gear stages), fast shaft with brake disc, generator 1,600 rpm, 2.00 MW, Cp 39 %; generator view (x-ray): a rotor of 8 magnets on the fast shaft spinning inside 12 still copper coils, where turning becomes electricity; gust to 34 mph (66-74 s): blades pitch to 10.5°, power held at 2.00 MW, Cp 15 %, tip speed 169 mph; storm: wind rises to 60 mph; cut-out at 56 mph (100.3 s), blades feather to 88° at 6°/s (close front view shows them go edge-on), power to 0, rotor slows 16 → 0 rpm by 115 s on a big rotor-speed gauge, then is braked; swept-area highlight: the 68,000 ft² circle and the half-size 17,000 ft² circle, with half-size power (a quarter). readouts: wind speed (mph), rotor rpm, rotor speed gauge (big rpm + BRAKE ON), generator rpm, power (kW / MW), power coefficient %, Betz limit 59 %, blade pitch °, tip speed mph, yaw error °, gear ratio 100 : 1, air speed at rotor and behind, power in the wind, swept area ft², half-size area and power. not in the model, never say it is shown: transformer, cable, power line, grid, converter, inverter, planetary, pitch motor, cooling, ladder, lift, lightning, ice, foundation, tilt, slip ring, battery, control cabinet. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=windturbine"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Moving air pushes the blades. Wind is moving air, and moving air carries energy. At 16 mph the air flowing through this rotor brings 1.34 MW. The blades are shaped like wings, so the wind makes them turn.","do":["set m view=front speed=1 mt=2 hi=wind labels=wind,blades"]},{"say":"Step 2: The air slows down. To take energy out, the rotor slows the air: from 16 mph to 13 mph at the blades and 11 mph behind them. The energy the air lost is what turns the rotor.","do":["set m view=side speed=1 hi=wind labels=wind,blades"]},{"say":"Step 3: A gearbox speeds it up. The big rotor turns slowly, 16 times a minute. Gears inside the gearbox make the fast shaft spin 100 times faster: 1,600 turns a minute. (Shown in slow motion.)","do":["set m view=nacelle xray=0.9 speed=0.1 mt=63 hi=mainShaft,gearbox labels=mainShaft,gearbox"]},{"say":"Step 4: Magnets spin inside coils. The fast shaft spins a ring of magnets inside still coils of copper wire. Moving magnets push electric current through the coils: this is where turning becomes electricity. Here it makes 2.00 MW.","do":["set m view=generator xray=0.9 speed=0.1 hi=coils labels=magnets,coils"]},{"say":"Step 5: It can never catch it all. In light wind this turbine turns 44 % of the wind's power into electricity. No turbine can pass 59 %, the Betz limit: the air must keep moving to get out of the way.","do":["set m view=front xray=0 speed=1 mt=10 hi= labels="]}]}

name: wing-3d
desc: 3D working model: lift, wing, airfoil, stall, angle of attack, flaps, takeoff, landing, Bernoulli. views: side threeq view top rear. parts: wing (Wing), leadingEdge (Leading edge), trailingEdge (Trailing edge), flap (Flap), aileron (Aileron), upperFlow (Air over the top), lowerFlow (Air underneath), downwash (Air pushed down), liftArrow (Lift), weight (Weight), pressureLow (Low pressure), pressureHigh (Higher pressure). effects: none. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: level 0-10, stall 10-26, takeoff 26-38. shows: faster, lower-pressure air over the top; higher pressure underneath; air pushed down behind the wing (downwash); lift and weight arrows that change with angle and speed; angle of attack rising to 15° (peak lift) and the stall at 18°; flaps lowering to 15° at takeoff speed, lift from 61% to 117% of weight. readouts: angle of attack, airspeed (mph), lift coefficient, lift (lb), lift as % of weight, flap angle. not in the model, never say it is shown: slat, spoiler, fuselage, tail, rudder, elevator, vortex, winglet, sliding flap, landing gear. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=wing"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: A wing in moving air. This is a slice of an airliner wing, 13 ft from front to back, with air rushing past. It is curved on top and tilted 2° nose-up.","do":["set m view=threeq speed=1 mt=0 labels=wing,leadingEdge,flap,aileron"]},{"say":"Step 2: The top air speeds up. Each dark column of dots started out together. Over the curved top the air speeds up and reaches the back first. It does not wait for the air underneath.","do":["set m view=side speed=0.6 mt=1 hi=upperFlow labels=upperFlow,lowerFlow"]},{"say":"Step 3: Fast air, low pressure. Where air speeds up, its pressure drops. So the air pushes up on the bottom of the wing harder than it pushes down on the top.","do":["set m speed=0.6 mt=2 hi=pressureLow,pressureHigh labels=pressureLow,pressureHigh"]},{"say":"Step 4: The air is pushed down. Behind the wing the air leaves aimed a little downward. The wing pushes air down, so the air pushes the wing up.","do":["set m speed=0.6 mt=3 hi=downwash labels=downwash"]},{"say":"Step 5: Lift equals weight. At 335 mph and 2°, the wing makes 174,000 lb of lift: 100% of the plane's weight. So it flies level.","do":["set m speed=0.6 mt=4 hi=liftArrow labels=liftArrow,weight"]}]}

name: wingshapes-3d
desc: 3D working model: wing shape, wing planform, straight wing, swept wing, delta wing, winglet, wing tip vortex, induced drag, lift to drag, aspect ratio, glider wing, sweep, Mach. views: lineup fast long tips tipClose. parts: straightWing (Straight wing), sweptWing (Swept wing), deltaWing (Delta wing), gliderWing (Long, skinny wing), plainTip (Plain wing tip), winglet (Winglet), tipVortex (Tip vortex), wingletVortex (Weaker tip vortex), smoke (Smoke line), acrossAir (Air crossing the wing), spanBar (Span), tipLeak (Air leaking round the tip). effects: none. clock: fixed windows, jump with mt: straight 0-10, swept 10-20, delta 20-30, long wing 30-40, plain tip 40-50, winglet 50-60, Mach race 60-86 (holds Mach .2 at 60-66, .78 at 69-76, 1.6 at 79-86), long vs straight 86-96. shows: straight, swept and delta wings side by side, same wing area; a long, skinny wing against a straight wing, same wing area; one wing with a plain tip on one side and a winglet on the other; tip vortices as a few smoke lines, tighter on short wings, gentler on long ones; air leaking round a wing tip from under the wing to the top; the part of the air that crosses a swept wing's edge (why sweep delays shock drag); best lift-to-drag of three shapes at Mach .2, .78 and 1.6. readouts: speed (mph), Mach, aspect ratio, sweep (°), Mach across the wing, best lift ÷ drag, induced drag (lb), tip swirl energy (%), glide from 1 mile up (mi), sink rate (ft/min). not in the model, never say it is shown: flap, slat, aileron, spoiler, tail, rudder, elevator, engine, propeller, fuselage, landing gear, shock wave, raked tip. example: {"els":{"m":"m3 id=wingshapes"},"steps":[{"say":"Step 1: Same area, three shapes. These wings have the same area. Each shape suits a different speed. We score them by lift ÷ drag: pounds of lift for each pound of drag.","do":["set m view=lineup speed=1 mt=1 labels=straightWing,sweptWing,deltaWing"]},{"say":"Step 2: Slow: straight is simple. At Mach .20, or 130 mph, the straight wing scores 18, as good as the swept wing, and it is lighter and easier to build. The stubby delta gets only 9.","do":["set m mt=60 hi=straightWing labels=straightWing"]},{"say":"Step 3: Near the speed of sound. At Mach .78, or 515 mph, air speeding over the top nears the speed of sound and drag jumps. The straight wing falls to 10. The swept wing holds 18.","do":["set m mt=69 hi=straightWing labels=straightWing,sweptWing"]},{"say":"Step 4: Why sweeping back helps. Only the air crossing the wing's edge square on matters. Sweep the wing 25° and it feels Mach .71 while the plane flies Mach .78. Slow flight pays for this: less lift.","do":["set m view=fast mt=11 hi=acrossAir,sweptWing labels=acrossAir"]},{"say":"Step 5: Faster than sound. At Mach 1.6, or 1,055 mph, the thin delta scores 6, the swept wing 4 and the straight wing 3. Every wing scores low, but the delta loses least.","do":["set m view=lineup mt=79 hi=deltaWing labels=deltaWing"]},{"say":"Step 6: Pick the shape for the job. Swept 60°, the delta feels only Mach .80 at Mach 1.6. No shape wins everywhere, so a plane's wing tells you how fast it was made to fly.","do":["set m view=fast mt=21 hi=acrossAir,deltaWing labels=acrossAir"]}]}
